bio.en: Naomi Gleit is Head of Product at Meta and, apart from Mark Zuckerberg, the longest-serving executive, having joined as employee #29 and scaled the company for nearly 20 years.
bio.zh: 娜奥米·格莱特（Naomi Gleit）是 Meta 的产品负责人，除马克·扎克伯格外任职最久的高管，她以第 29 号员工身份加入，伴随公司成长近 20 年。

summary.en: Naomi stresses creating a single "canonical doc" for every project to drive extreme clarity and avoid conflicting answers. She shares lessons from Meta's legendary early growth team and how to ramp up fast on any new initiative. The episode is a rare, practical master class in product leadership from inside Meta's senior ranks.
summary.zh: 娜奥米强调为每个项目建立唯一的"权威文档"（canonical doc），以实现极度清晰、避免答案相互矛盾。她分享了 Meta 传奇早期增长团队的经验，以及如何快速上手任何新项目。本期是一份来自 Meta 高层的罕见而实用的产品领导力大师课。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity. I work on a lot of different projects. A lot of times I'm ramping up a new project, I'm like, "Where can I learn what I need to learn about this project?" I ask five different people, get five different answers. That is unacceptable. Of course, I'm sure there's hundreds of docs associated with the project, but there needs to be one canonical doc. Everyone should know exactly where the canonical doc is. That's the one place I can go to get all the information I need about a project and it will link to all the other docs, things on the canonical doc are.
turns.zh: 我真心相信框架的力量，它能带来极致的清晰。我参与很多不同的项目。很多时候我刚接手一个新项目，就会想："我该去哪里了解这个项目需要掌握的东西？"我问五个不同的人，得到五个不同的答案。这是不可接受的。当然，我知道这个项目肯定关联着成百上千份文档，但必须有一份权威文档（canonical doc）。每个人都该确切知道那份权威文档在哪里。那是获取项目所有所需信息的唯一去处，它会链接到所有其他文档，权威文档上的内容就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny

She's seen the company scale from 30 employees to the one and a half trillion dollar business that it is today. Naomi does very few podcasts and interviews and so I was really excited to chat with her and have her on this podcast. In our conversation, we dig into the many lessons that she learned from Facebook's early and legendary growth team, her superpower of taking really complex and gnarly problems and projects, simplifying them and delivering results. We also get into leadership lessons she's learned from Zuck, including his recent transformation into possibly the coolest CEO in tech. Also, why PMs are the conductor of product teams, some very tactical tips for running meetings, writing docs, working out, getting better sleep, and even how to get more protein in your diet. turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Facebook as part of being an academic, researching Facebook, also being a Stanford student using Facebook. I was like, "I really want to work here." Facebook had just moved to Palo Alto. Mark had driven across country I guess, and arrived in Palo. Alto opened up an office at 443 Emerson Avenue or Emerson Street. It was right above the Jing Jing's Chinese restaurant in downtown Palo Alto and I just went to the office sort of cold called the equivalent of just walking into the office and seeing if there were any available jobs. There were not. I think I did that maybe five to 10 more times. (00:07:31): Eventually, there was an opening to interview for Sean Parker's personal assistant. He was at the time I think the president. I did interview and I did not get the job. A few months later I found out about a marketing role that was available. And one interesting thing I haven't really talked about was I got an offer from Facebook. I also got a competing offer from LinkedIn, and so at that time I made the choice to go to Facebook because I was interested in the social networking aspect of it. Why was I so bullish on this website at the time it was www.thefacebook.com. Why was I so excited about this thing? (00:08:12): I think it's because I definitely saw that there was product market fit. I saw that students at Stanford were obsessed with it, but it also had a long list of colleges that were really excited and on the waiting list to be accepted onto Facebook, and so there was this product market fit piece and also a huge demand from other audiences, other colleges, but our younger brothers and sisters were also sort of interested about Facebook and it seemed like it had this much broader appeal. So that's what happened. I got the marketing job. Cheryl also talks about when you are on getting a rocket ship, don't ask what seat. That was my foot in the door and here we are 19 years later.
turns.zh: 我当时作为学者在研究 Facebook，同时作为斯坦福学生也在用 Facebook。我就想："我真的好想来这里工作。"Facebook 当时刚搬到帕洛阿尔托。Mark 应该是开车横穿了整个国家，到了帕洛阿尔托，在 Emerson 大道 443 号（或者叫 Emerson 街）开了个办公室。就在帕洛阿尔托市中心 Jing Jing 中餐馆的正上方，我就直接去了办公室，算是"冷拜访"——相当于直接走进去问问有没有空缺职位。当时没有。我想我又去了大概五到十次。(00:07:31)：后来终于有一个给 Sean Parker 当私人助理的面试机会。他当时应该是总裁。我去面试了，但没拿到那个职位。几个月后，我得知有一个市场岗位的空缺。还有一件我之前没怎么讲过的有趣事：我当时拿到了 Facebook 的 offer，同时也拿到了 LinkedIn 的竞争性 offer，所以我当时选择去 Facebook，是因为我对它的社交网络属性更感兴趣。为什么我当时对这个网站这么看好？它当时还是 www.thefacebook.com。我为什么对这东西这么兴奋？(00:08:12)：我想是因为我确实看到了产品市场契合（product-market fit）。我看到斯坦福的学生对它非常着迷，而且它还有一长串非常兴奋、在等待名单上等着被接纳进入 Facebook 的大学，所以既有产品市场契合这一点，又有来自其他受众、其他高校的庞大需求，甚至连我们的弟弟妹妹们也对 Facebook 有点兴趣，看起来它有更广泛的吸引力。事情就是这样。我拿到了市场岗。Cheryl 也说过，当你搭上一艘火箭飞船时，别问坐哪个座位。那是我踏进门的一步，而 19 年后的今天，我们依然在这里。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yeah, it was pure just refusing to quit. I think I just walked into the office, I talked to the person at the front desk, "Is there anything that I can do?" They weren't hiring non-technical people. I didn't have a computer science degree. I wasn't technical. I had this bachelor of arts degree and that's why the personal assistant in the marketing role eventually did open and was something that I thought I could be qualified for.
turns.zh: 对，就是纯粹的死磕、绝不放弃。我就走进办公室，跟前台说："有什么我能做的吗？"当时他们不招非技术岗的人。我没有计算机科学学位，不是技术出身。我只有文学学士学位，所以后来私人助理和市场岗开放了，我觉得那是自己够资格做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. I think that's such an empowering lesson of if you look at someone like you and they're like, "Oh, she was so early at Facebook, how lucky," clearly wasn't luck. You knew you wanted to work at this company. You put a lot of effort into making it happen no matter the job. I think that's a really good takeaway and lesson. So if there's a company today that you are excited about that you're just like, "This is going to be a massive success," what I'm hearing is just do everything you can to try to land a job there and eventually you'll be in a role you actually want. It doesn't have to start there.
turns.zh: 酷。我觉得这是个非常赋予力量的教训：当你看到像你这样的人，别人说"哦，她好早就进了 Facebook，好幸运"，但显然不是幸运。你当时就知道自己想在 Facebook 工作，你付出了巨大努力去实现它，不管什么岗位。我觉得这是个很好的收获和教训。所以，如果今天有一家让你兴奋、让你觉得"这一定会大获成功"的公司，我听到的是：尽你所能去那里谋一份工作，最终你会得到一个自己真正想要的岗位。它不必从那个岗位开始。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: When I got to Facebook, I knew I wanted to build. As someone who wasn't really technical, I wasn't going to be an engineer or a coder. I wanted to work with the engineers and the coders to build products. I thought product management was the right function for me, and so my dream was always to be a PM and it wasn't luck as to how I ended up becoming a PM. I sort of took the same approach showing up at the office asking if there were any roles. (00:11:08): By then, we had moved to 156 University and all of the PMs and engineers worked on the second floor, and I was working in marketing, like I mentioned, and I worked on the third floor and all the business functions worked on the third floor, and my goal was to be a PM. I ended up going, sort of the analogy, I went to the second floor most days after work, asked if there were any projects that I could help out with. (00:11:34): It was very early days. There was always more to do than people to do it. And so eventually I picked up a few projects, helping with program management, giving my product feedback, and by the time that I actually applied formally to be a product manager, I had been doing the job voluntarily, almost informally for a few months. (00:11:58): And I remember this because I had a seat on the third floor. I picked up all the stuff on my desk, put it in a box, walked down to the second floor once I got the job to become a PM. And when I got to the second floor, I distinctly remember everyone on the second floor standing and clapping. And so it was a big standing ovation. I'll never forget, Boz was there, by the way. I know Boz has been on your podcast, but even Boz was there sort of standing and clapping. And so I guess to the lesson that you were trying to extract from my story, I do think I sort of tried to create the luck by not giving up and just repeatedly cold calling or cold showing up or cold volunteering until I sort of was able to make it happen.
turns.zh: 我刚到 Facebook 时，就知道自己想做构建类的工作。作为一个不算真正技术出身的人，我不会去当工程师或程序员。我想和工程师、程序员一起打造产品。我觉得产品管理（PM）是适合我的职能，所以我一直以来的梦想就是当一名 PM，而我最终成为 PM 绝非运气。我用了同样的方式——出现在办公室，问有没有什么职位空缺。(00:11:08)：那时我们已经搬到了 156 University，所有 PM 和工程师都在二楼办公，而我像我说的那样在市场部，在三楼，所有业务职能都在三楼，而我的目标是成为 PM。结果我——打个比方——下班后大多数日子都往二楼跑，问有没有什么项目我能帮上忙的。(00:11:34)：那是非常早期的阶段。永远是有做不完的事、却没人手去做。所以最终我接了几个项目，帮忙做项目管理、给产品提反馈，等我正式申请成为产品经理时，我已经志愿地、近乎非正式地干了几个月这份工作了。(00:11:58)：我记得这个，因为我在三楼有个座位。我把桌上所有东西收进一个箱子，拿到 PM 录用通知后就走到了二楼。到了二楼，我清楚地记得二楼所有人起立鼓掌。那是一场盛大的起立致敬。我永远不会忘，顺便说一句，Boz 当时也在场。我知道 Boz 上过你的播客，就连 Boz 也站在那里鼓掌。所以，回到你想从我的故事里提炼的教训，我觉得我确实是靠不放弃、反复地冷电话、冷上门、冷志愿，直到我把它变成现实，才创造了那份运气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Again, very empowering. It's not just like, "Oh, there's these people that just get lucky they land this PM job." It's like you landed at the company. I want to be a product manager, which is interesting. Most people don't grow up in I want to be a product manager. That's like a rare thing people even want, especially that early on. So it's interesting that you already knew that, but you basically did the job. You did the job of PM before you had the job, and by the time you actually asked for it, you've been doing it for a long time and you could show, "Hey, look, I'm actually good at this. I can do this job." Awesome. (00:13:22): By the way, I love the Boz connection. I'm finding that Boz is connected to the most guests of this podcast in so many different ways.
turns.zh: 太了不起了。再一次，非常赋予力量。这不像"哦，就是那些运气好、一头撞进 PM 职位的人"。而是你先进了公司，然后说"我想做产品经理"，这点很有意思。大多数人并不是从小就想"我要当产品经理"。那是很罕见、连早期都很少有人想要的志向。所以你当时就已经知道这点很有意思，但你基本上是先干了这份活。在拿到职位之前，你就已经在做 PM 的活了，等你真正开口要的时候，你已经干了很久，可以证明"嘿，看，我其实很擅长这个，我能做这份工作"。真棒。(00:13:22)：顺便说，我超爱 Boz 这个连接。我发现 Boz 以各种方式和这档播客的绝大多数嘉宾都有牵连。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Curious. Yeah, like Ami and-
turns.zh: 好奇。对，比如 Ami 和——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a few other people. It's just interesting. There's a Boz spiderweb of connections throughout this podcast so far. Okay, so I'm going to fast-forward to today. So your role today is head of product at Meta?
turns.zh: 还有另外几个人。就是很有意思。到目前为止，这档播客里有一张 Boz 的关系蛛网。好，我要快进到今天了。所以你今天的角色是 Meta 的产品负责人？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does that mean? What do you do at Meta today? How would you describe your role?
turns.zh: 那是什么意思？你今天在 Meta 具体做什么？你会怎么描述你的角色？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: There are a few thousand PMs at Meta. They do not all report to me. I would say a few hundred of them report to me on the teams that I directly manage, but I feel responsible for the entire PM community at Meta. There are things that we do centrally, things like PM performance, PM culture PM onboarding and training, and that's the kind of thing that I look out for. (00:14:16): Obviously I wanted to be a PM. Head of product is my dream job. I am deeply supportive of the PM function, and so I really care and I think PMs are a huge point of leverage in a company for how we can actually get stuff done and help accomplish the company's goals. And so I sort of focus on PM as a really important exponential lever for doing that.
turns.zh: Meta 有几千名 PM。他们并不都向我汇报。我直接管理的团队里大概有几百名 PM 向我汇报，但我觉得自己对 Meta 整个 PM 群体都负有责任。我们会做一些集中化的事情，比如 PM 的绩效、PM 文化、PM 的入职和培训，这类事就是我关注的范围。(00:14:16)：显然，我当初想当 PM。产品负责人是我梦想的工作。我对 PM 这个职能有着深切的支持，所以我真的非常在意，我认为 PM 是公司里一个巨大的杠杆点，能帮我们真正把事情做成、助力实现公司目标。所以我某种程度上把 PM 当作一个非常重要的指数级杠杆来聚焦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay. I'm going to come back to what you've learned about what makes super successful PMs, what makes you really successful. I want to take a tangent to Zuck.
turns.zh: 我爱这个。好。我想回头再聊你学到的最成功的 PM 具备什么特质、是什么让你如此成功。我想先岔开去聊聊 Zuck。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Please. Yes.
turns.zh: 请便。好啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you've known Zuck for over 20 years at this point, and I just have to ask a few Zuck questions because people are always curious to learn from what has worked so well for him. The first question is just there's been a pretty profound transformation in Mark over the past few years, both in terms of how he leads and also just in his coolness and vibe factor. What are your thoughts on just this transformation and how he's been able to pull it off?
turns.zh: 所以你认识 Zuck 到现在已经超过 20 年了，我必须问几个 Zuck 的问题，因为大家一直很好奇能从他行之有效的做法中学到什么。第一个问题就是，过去几年 Mark 发生了相当深刻的转变，无论在他领导的方式上，还是在他那种酷劲和氛围感上。你怎么看这种转变，以及他是怎么做到的呢？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: So I've always said that there is the biggest gap of anybody I know between what people think of Mark and who Mark really is. And so I think this is the Mark that I've known for the past 20 years and the world is finally getting to see what I've been lucky enough to see. And that gap that we've talked about is really starting to close. (00:15:46): How did we get here? I always say Mark is a learn it all, not a know-it-all. He is the fastest person at upskilling of anyone I've ever met. He used to do these annual challenges. One year I did them with him, it was learning Chinese, and within a year he was able to basically achieve an eighth grade fluency in Chinese. And that's just one example. Obviously, he's gotten incredibly great at guitar, MMA, a lot of his passions, but he's also gotten a lot better at some of the professional skills. And I think negotiation, public speaking is one of those. I think before in the early days, it just wasn't something that he was very comfortable with. He's talked himself about coming across as a little scripted. I think he was not confident and pretty careful about how he showed up and he's upskilled here. He's just gotten a lot more comfortable, and so people are able to see who he really is.
turns.zh: 我总是说，在我认识的人里，关于 Mark 的公众印象与他真实的样子之间，落差最大。所以我觉得这就是我过去 20 年认识的那个 Mark，而世界终于开始看到我有幸一直看到的样子了。我们说的那个落差真的在开始缩小。(00:15:46)：我们是怎么走到今天的？我总说 Mark 是个"学习者"（learn it all），而不是"什么都懂的人"（know-it-all）。他是我见过提升自我技能最快的人。他以前会做那些年度挑战。有一年我和他一起做，是学中文，结果一年内他基本达到了八年级的中文流利水平。这只是一个例子。显然，他在吉他、MMA 综合格斗等很多爱好上都变得极其厉害，但他在一些职业技能上也变强了很多。我觉得谈判能力、公开演讲就是其中之一。我想早期那并不是他特别舒服的事。他自己也说过，当时显得有点像照本宣科。我觉得他当时不自信，对自己怎么亮相非常谨慎，而他在这些方面提升了。他变得自在得多，于是人们能看到他真实的一面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He was also like, I don't know, 20 something when he started Facebook and now he's running a 80,000 person org. I could see the emotion habits.
turns.zh: 他当时开始做 Facebook 的时候，也就二十出头吧，现在他管理着 8 万人的组织。我能想象到那种情绪习惯的变化。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes. I think he might've been 19 or 20 when I came.
turns.zh: 对。我想我刚去的时候他可能才 19 或 20 岁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh God, that's insane. So yeah, I could see why someone would change. I was at the Acquired podcast Chase event with him being interviewed, and he's just such a cool dude now. He just has these big shirts with his own letters on it, his own phrases, his chain. What a cool dude.
turns.zh: 天哪，太疯狂了。所以是啊，我能理解一个人会怎么改变。我当时在 Acquired 播客的 Chase 活动上，看他接受采访，他现在就是个超酷的家伙。他穿着印着自己字母、自己口头禅的大 T 恤，戴着链子。真是个酷哥。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: His long hair.
turns.zh: 他的长头发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: His long hair.
turns.zh: 他的长头发。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: His watch. Yeah, I was at that event too. I thought it was great. I think, yeah, that's the no gap between who Mark is and what the world sees.
turns.zh: 他的手表。对，那个活动我也在。我觉得很棒。我想说，没错，这就是 Mark 真实的样子和世人看到的样子之间，已经没有落差了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Is there something about Zuck that you know that most people don't know? Something that would surprise us?
turns.zh: 我爱这个。关于 Zuck，有没有什么是你知道、但大多数人不知道的？什么会让我们惊讶的？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: The one thing I would say about Mark is I think people know he's married. He has three daughters. He's a really great dad, he's a really great husband. I would say he's also a really good friend. Maybe that's something that I can sort of speak to from experience. He's just an incredibly thoughtful friend. There was a period in my life, I think it was 10 years ago when I was going through just sort of a really hard time. I had come out of a breakup, but Mark saw that I was having a hard time. He asked me if I wanted to volunteer to teach a class in East Palo Alto after their school day. (00:18:15): And in retrospect, it's pretty funny, but Mark and I taught a class about how to build a business. So you had the CEO of Meta teaching this class to a bunch of middle school students, and we got really close to them through that process. We made some really important mentorship connections. For years, we met with them. I think we still continue to, even though they've now at this point graduated from college and have real jobs. (00:18:43): But one of the lessons that we taught during that class that I remember Mark distinctly writing on the whiteboard, or not the whiteboard, there actually was chalk, it was with chalk on a chalkboard with the four life lessons. That was one, and I kept these for myself as well, love yourself. Two, only then can you truly serve others. Three, focus on what you can control. And four, for those things never give up. (00:19:12): And that was sort of his life lessons, four steps to how to approach life. And we actually made stickers for these four steps that the students could actually put on their composition notebooks as a reminder. And I think obviously that has really helped me over time, but I think that in that you can see some of what I think we all see in Mark, for example, for those things never give up. He has that aspect of him and it makes sense. For me number three is really the hardest, which is focus on what you can control. I think I probably think I can control more things than I actually can.
turns.zh: 关于 Mark，我想说的一点是，大家知道他结婚了，有三个女儿。他是个非常好的爸爸、非常好的丈夫。我还想说，他也是个非常好的朋友。也许这是我凭亲身经历能说上几句的事。他就是个极其体贴的朋友。我人生中有段时间——大概是十年前——正经历一段特别艰难的时期。我刚结束一段恋情，Mark 看出我过得不好。他问我愿不愿意在放学后，去东帕洛阿尔托的一所学校志愿教一门课。(00:18:15)：事后想想还挺好笑的，但 Mark 和我教了一门关于"怎么创业"的课。于是 Meta 的 CEO 在给一群初中生上课，而我们通过那个过程和他们变得非常亲近，建立了一些非常重要的导师连接。多年来我们一直和他们见面。我想即使现在，他们都已经大学毕业、有了正经工作，我们还在继续。(00:18:43)：但那门课里我们教的一条经验，我清楚地记得 Mark 用粉笔写在黑板上（不是白板，当时是真的粉笔），是四条人生教训：一，爱自己；二，只有这样你才能真正服务他人；三，专注你能控制的事；四，对这些事永不放弃。(00:19:12)：那算是他的人生教训，关于如何对待生活的四个步骤。我们真的给这四个步骤做了贴纸，让学生可以贴在笔记本上提醒自己。我想这显然多年来帮了我很多，而我觉得从中你能看到我们都在 Mark 身上看到的某些特质，比如"对这些事永不放弃"。他有这一面，这很合理。对我来说，第三条最难，就是"专注你能控制的事"。我想我大概总觉得自己能控制的比实际能控制的更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So do we all. I love that he was sharing that in a class on how to start a business, this life advice.
turns.zh: 我们也是。我好爱他居然在"怎么创业"的课上分享这种人生建议。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, that's amazing. I want to chat a bit about, so at this point is 86,000 employees, something like that. That's what I found online. So he has to run this massive org as this CEO, one person. I know that one way that he does this, he has something called a small group. Is that the term?
turns.zh: 哦天，太了不起了。我想聊一点，你现在公司大概 86,000 名员工，我在网上查到的是这个数。所以他得以 CEO 一己之力管理这个庞大的组织。我知道他这么做的一个方式是，他有个叫 small group（小团队）的东西。是这么叫的吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes, small group.
turns.zh: 对，small group（小团队）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So he's got the small group that he calls it and it's essentially is like core execs and this group meets regularly, and that's kind of how he's able to manage the entire org through this small group. For people that are struggling to run an increasingly larger org, are there any tidbits from how Mark and the small group operate that might be helpful to folks?
turns.zh: 好，酷。所以他有个叫 small group 的团队，本质上就是核心高管，这个团队定期开会，他大致就是通过这个小团队来管理整个组织。对于那些正在艰难管理一个越来越大的组织的人，Mark 和小团队运作方式里，有没有什么可能对大家有用的小窍门？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Sure. So I think the first thing is small group is sort of the leadership team. It's the leaders working on the most important projects at the company, sort of independent of reporting structure and stuff. It's like who are the leaders on the big most important projects or functions? They will be represented in small group. (00:21:08): What makes this group unique? A lot of them are people like me, people that have been there for a very long time. So I think the tenure of small group is really rare. Why I think that's important is you have a lot of people that are motivated by mission rather than climbing the corporate ladder at this point. And so there are a lot of what I call disagreeable givers. (00:21:34): So just to back up, I don't know if you've heard this framework, but I think I learned this from Adam Grant during an executive learning and development session, and he was saying that if you think of a two-by-two, there's people who are agreeable and disagreeable, and then there's people who are givers and takers. (00:21:52): And the most dangerous kind of person to have in an organization is an agreeable taker. And what that means is an agreeable person, super nice, everyone likes them, really easy to get along with, but they're a taker and maybe their motivation is more self-interested rather than what's best for the company, which is how I would define a giver. And the most precious person in an organization is the disagreeable giver. Those are the people who are really motivated to do what's best for the company, but they can be a little bit disagreeable in the sense that they may not say what you want to hear. They may push back on things, they may fight for things. And so I think small group is characterized by a lot of disagreeable givers and I think that's really important for an organization. (00:22:41): One thing I think Mark has done really well in general is just have a culture, including on his leadership team, of people who give him feedback. I think a lot of times as you get more successful or as you have more fame or if you have more wealth, you lose having an accurate feedback loop. And people may not want to be a hundred percent honest with you for various reasons. And Mark has tried to ensure that he himself has an accurate feedback loop, or we as a company have more of an accurate feedback loop by surrounding himself and our leadership team and creating a culture of giving direct and honest feedback. So that's some of the unique properties of small group. (00:23:25): From a process perspective, we have one weekly sort of strategic meeting. It's more open-ended, there is time for discussion. It's longer and it's sort of more unstructured. We also have one weekly operational meeting, which is highly structured where we go through all of the priority projects. The person who owns each of the projects will actually speak to the weekly updates for that project. And it's very operational and tactical.
turns.zh: 当然。我觉得第一点是，small group 某种程度上就是领导团队。是在公司最重要项目上工作的人，某种程度上与汇报关系无关。也就是：那些最重要项目或职能的负责人是谁？他们就会在 small group 里有代表。(00:21:08)：这个团队有什么特别？他们中有很多像我这样的人，在那儿待了很久的人。所以我觉得 small group 的任职时长非常罕见。我觉得这重要的原因是，到了这个阶段，很多人是被使命驱动，而不是为了爬公司阶梯。所以有很多我所谓的"不好相处但乐于付出的人"（disagreeable givers）。(00:21:34)：先退一步说，我不知道你有没有听过这个框架，但我是在一次高管学习发展课上从 Adam Grant 那儿学的。他说如果你画一个 2x2，一边是"随和／不随和"，另一边是"付出型／索取型"。(00:21:52)：组织里最危险的人是"随和且索取型"。意思是：一个随和的人，超级好、大家都喜欢、特别好相处，但他是索取型的，他的动机可能更偏私利，而不是对公司最有利——我就是这样定义"付出型"的。而组织里最珍贵的人是"不随和但付出型"。这些人真正被"做对公司最有利的事"驱动，但他们可能有点不随和，因为他们未必会说你想听的话。他们可能会反对、会为某些事抗争。所以我觉得 small group 的特征就是有大量"不随和但付出型"的人，而我认为这对一个组织真的很重要。(00:22:41)：我觉得 Mark 整体上做得很好的一件事，就是营造一种文化——包括在他的领导团队里——让人们给他反馈。我觉得很多时候，当你越成功、名气越大、财富越多，你就越难拥有准确的反馈回路。人们可能因为各种原因不愿意 100% 对你坦诚。而 Mark 努力确保他自己、也确保我们公司作为整体拥有更准确的反馈回路，方法是让自己和领导团队被这样的人围绕，并营造一种给予直接、诚实反馈的文化。这就是 small group 的一些独特之处。(00:23:25)：从流程角度看，我们每周有一个偏战略性的会议，比较开放，有时间讨论，时间更长、更 unstructured（非结构化）。我们每周还有一个运营会议，高度结构化，会过一遍所有优先项目。每个项目的负责人会亲自汇报该项目本周的进展。非常运营化、非常战术化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I just love this name, small group. It's just like a cozy name. It's not like executive staff or ESA after all these terms people always use. And that's just our small group.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我就爱 small group 这个名字，像个很温馨的名字。不是什么"执行参谋"或"ESA"那些人们总用的词。就是我们的 small group。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then this framework you described, it sounds a lot like radical candor of challenging directly, but caring deeply.
turns.zh: 然后你描述的这个框架，听起来很像"激进坦诚"（radical candor）——直接挑战，但深深关怀。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where being disagreeable, but being constructive and additive. Is that the term? What was it? Disagreeable, but?
turns.zh: 就是"不随和，但建设性、有增益"。是这么叫吗？那叫什么来着？不随和，但是？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: A giver.
turns.zh: 付出型（a giver）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Giver? Yeah.
turns.zh: 付出型（giver）？对。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That's great.
turns.zh: 好。那很棒。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If there's nothing here, totally cool. But is there something that you changed Mark's mind about? You've talked about he's good at seeing new data and being like, "Oh, okay, I see, I see." Or is there anything that you were successful there that is an interesting story?
turns.zh: 如果这里没什么可讲的也完全没关系。但你有没有改过 Mark 主意的某件事？你说过他擅长看到新数据就说"哦，好，我懂了，我懂了"。或者有没有什么你成功说服他的、有意思的故事？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: One of the things that we did in the early days on the growth team, because I'm not sure that necessarily when we talk about this sort of legacy or the history or the lore around the growth team, and this may not be a direct answer to the question, but it didn't really necessarily-
turns.zh: 早期我们在增长团队做的一件事里，因为我不确信这到底算不算对那个问题的直接回答，但增长团队的这段传奇、历史或传闻，可能并不——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: And this may not be a direct answer to the question, but it didn't really necessarily come from Mark. Mark wasn't like, "You guys should create a growth team. Here's how you should operate." And so I think in some ways we established and grew a growth team and Mark got on board or saw the value in it and was a huge proponent of it, but I'm not sure it necessarily originated with him. And indeed, I think sometimes the focus on being so data- driven might've been something that myself, Alex Schultz, Javier Olavon, these are some of the original people that were on the growth team and that my closest coworkers now may have really pushed on and highlighted the value of for Mark. I'm happy to talk about the growth team, which is something I get asked a lot of questions about, if you want.
turns.zh: 这可能不是对那个问题的直接回答，但它其实并非真的来自 Mark。Mark 并没有说"你们应该建一个增长团队，这是你们该怎么运作"。所以在某些方面，是我们建立并壮大了增长团队，Mark 后来认同了、看到了它的价值、成了它的大力支持者，但我不确定它一定起源于他。事实上，我觉得有时候那种对"如此数据驱动"的强调，可能是我自己、Alex Schultz、Javier Olavon——这些是增长团队最早的一些人，也是我现在最亲密的同事——真正推动并凸显给 Mark 的价值。如果你愿意，我很乐意聊聊增长团队，这是大家经常问我的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'd love to. That's exactly where I was about to segue since you brought that up. So the Facebook growth team, it's a legendary team. I think it was probably the first real growth team in tech. The team developed some of the most core growth levers and techniques that companies use today, and so I'm really excited to chat a bit about this and what you learned from that time. One thing I wanted to start with is there's this legendary activation metric that you all had, the goal was to get, I think it was seven friends in 10 days or something like that. Is that a real thing? Is that what you guys actually did? Anything more there for folks that are like, "Oh, we got to come up with something like this"?
turns.zh: 好啊，我很想听。你刚提到这个，我正要转过去。Facebook 的增长团队，是一支传奇的团队。我想它大概是科技圈第一支真正的增长团队。这支团队开发了一些如今各公司仍在使用的最核心的增长杠杆和技巧，所以我非常兴奋能聊一聊这个，以及你从那段时期学到的东西。我想先聊的一点是，你们当时有个传奇的激活指标，目标是让用户——我想是——10 天内加 7 个好友之类？这是真事吗？你们当时真这么做了？对于那种"哦，我们也得搞个这样的东西"的人，还有没有更多可说的？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Sure. So yes, seven friends in 10 days was a thing. 10 friends in 14 days was also a thing. They're the same thing, they're just different points on a retention curve. I would say the key insight here is when we started the growth team, I think we were pretty focused on acquisition. We had a notion though of growth accounting, which looks at what's our net growth every day? And that would look at the number of new users that registered minus the number of users that actually went stale. So after a 30-day period, that's how we define it, they no longer logged in. And then plus the number of users that resurrected, which is after 30 days they came back. And what we found was the churn in resurrection lines were actually much larger than the new user line, which implied to us that retention and driving those two lines was actually our biggest lever to drive net growth. (00:27:22): And so while we were focused on acquisition, a lot of our focus shifted to be around engagement and retention. How do we drive engagement and retention? We look at the variables that correlate most with that outcome. What we found was friending. And so those two magic moments, having seven friends in 10 days or 10 friends in 14 days really just map to when we feel like your likelihood of being a retained user goes up because you've seen the value in Facebook. And it makes sense, Facebook is much more compelling if you have 14 friends. And the other thing around 10 or 14 days is we wanted it to happen quickly, we wanted to have you experience the magic moment soon after you had registered on the site to prevent you from churning and then us having to resurrect you again.
turns.zh: 当然。是的，10 天内 7 个好友是一回事。14 天内 10 个好友也是一回事。它们是一回事，只是留存曲线上不同的点。我想这里的关键洞察是：当我们刚开始增长团队时，我觉得我们相当聚焦于获客（acquisition）。但我们当时有个"增长核算"（growth accounting）的概念，看的是我们每天净增长是多少？那就是新注册用户数，减去真正流失的用户数。我们定义的是：30 天后他们不再登录，就算流失。再加上"复活"的用户数，也就是 30 天后又回来的。我们发现流失线和复活线其实比新用户线大得多，这就暗示我们：留存和推动那两条线才是驱动净增长最大的杠杆。(00:27:22)：所以虽然我们聚焦获客，但我们的注意力大量转移到了参与度和留存上。我们怎么驱动参与度和留存？我们看与这个结果相关性最高的变量。我们发现是"加好友"。所以那两个神奇时刻——10 天内 7 个好友，或 14 天内 10 个好友——其实就对应着：当你已经看到 Facebook 的价值时，你成为留存用户的可能性就上升了。这很合理，如果你有 14 个好友，Facebook 会吸引人得多。而 10 天或 14 天这点，是我们希望它尽快发生，希望你在注册网站后很快体验到那个神奇时刻，防止你流失、然后我们又要去"复活"你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the most interesting lessons from this activation metric that people talk about, because right now everyone's like, "Yeah, of course retention is what you need to focus on. That's what product-market fit is." I think right now that's what everyone knows. I love that you guys basically figured that out, was one of the first times of, "Here's how we understand if our product will last and how to grow retention because it matters most." And retention cohort curves I think was one of the innovations y'all thought about early of just like, "Here's how we track retention, people joining at a certain time, how long do they stick around?"
turns.zh: 从这个激活指标里，人们聊到的最有意思的教训之一是：现在大家都说"对啊，当然留存才是你该聚焦的，那就是产品市场契合"。我想现在这是人尽皆知的。我超爱你们基本上把这件事想明白了，是最早一批"我们靠这个理解产品能不能持久、怎么提升留存因为它最关键"的人。留存队列曲线（retention cohort curves）我想也是你们早期就想出来的创新之一——就是"我们怎么追踪留存：某段时间加入的人，能待多久？"

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally. And that was Danny Ferrante who really came up with the growth accounting framework, which I guess is quite obvious, but the plus new minus stale plus resurrected. The thing that I feel like may be valuable for PMs and is one of my Naomi-isms is I think what the growth team really pioneered was being data-driven and product-driven, especially in an area that was historically more of a business function. So I think at that time a lot of the growth in new users was expected to come from marketing or comms, whereas the insight that we had is actually the product is the biggest lever to drive growth, and that means we should have a product and engineering team working on optimizing things like the registration flow, the invite flow, the new user onboarding, getting you seven friends in 10 days. (00:29:43): One of my Naomi-isms is really understand, identify, and execute. That framework came from 2009 where the growth team at the time, it was fledgling and it just started, was focused on only instrumenting data. And Alex often wears a shirt that says, "I guess when you can know." We just didn't have the data that we needed to make informed decisions to know really what were the biggest levers to drive growth. And so in 2009 in January, we basically stopped doing anything on our roadmap except data instrumentation. And that's when we instrumented every step of the registration flow, instrumented every step of the news or onboarding experience. We knew where there was drop off. And so we understood, which allowed us to identify what were the key opportunities to drive growth and maybe, hey, it's increasing friending in the user experience or 20% drop off on registered users at the email confirmation step, how can we address that? These are the opportunities that we identified and then we would execute by building products. (00:30:50): So having this data-driven product-driven approach to what I think historically was more of a business responsibility at a company was sort of the special sauce of the growth team. We eventually extended that approach. I think that approach started with the growth team, but we extended to other areas. So for example, one of the projects that I took on after growth was social impact. And instead of what I think a normal company might do, which is start a corporate social responsibility wing, we decided, no, we're going to take a data-driven product-driven approach to driving social impact. Instead of having a foundation that's distributing money, we're going to build a product that actually raises money from our community. And many years later we've raised billions of dollars from the community for charity. So that's sort of the approach that I think is unique about the growth team that expanded to other areas and that I think that the company in many ways has taken to most of the problems that we face.
turns.zh: 完全同意。那是 Danny Ferrante 真正提出"增长核算"框架的，我想这挺显然的，就是加新减流失加复活。我觉得对 PM 有价值、也是我的 Naomi-isms 之一的是：增长团队真正开创的，是在一个历史上更偏业务职能的领域里，做到"数据驱动"和"产品驱动"。所以我想当时很多新用户的增长被预期来自市场或公关，而我们的洞察是：实际上产品才是驱动增长最大的杠杆，这意味着我们应该有一个产品和工程团队，去优化注册流程、邀请流程、新用户引导，让你在 10 天内加 7 个好友。(00:29:43)：我的一个 Naomi-ism 是：理解（understand）、识别（identify）、执行（execute）。这个框架来自 2009 年，当时增长团队刚起步、还很稚嫩，只聚焦于埋点数据。Alex 常穿一件写着"当你能量化时，你才能知道"（I guess when you can know）的 T 恤。我们当时就是没有做明智决策、真正搞清驱动增长最大杠杆所需的数据。所以 2009 年 1 月，我们基本上停掉了路线图上的其他一切，只做数据埋点。那是我们埋点了注册流程的每一步、动态或引导体验的每一步。我们清楚哪里有流失。(00:30:50)：于是我们"理解"了，这让我们能"识别"哪些是驱动增长的关键机会——比如，是不是提升用户体验里的加好友，或者注册用户在邮件确认步骤有 20% 的流失，怎么解决？这些都是我们识别出的机会，然后我们通过打造产品来"执行"。所以把这种数据驱动、产品驱动的方法，用在我认为历史上更属于公司业务职责的地方，就是增长团队的独门秘方。我们后来把这个方法延伸了。我想这个方法始于增长团队，但我们延伸到了其他领域。比如，我在增长之后接手的一个项目是"社会影响"（social impact）。我们没有像正常公司那样去开一个企业社会责任部门，而是决定：不，我们要用数据驱动、产品驱动的方式来做社会影响。与其搞一个撒钱基金会，我们要打造一个真正从社区筹款的产品。多年后，我们已经通过社区为慈善筹到了数十亿美元。所以这就是增长团队独特的方法，它扩展到了其他领域，而公司在很多方面也把它用到了我们面对的大部分问题上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point. And I almost took that for granted, but there was such a huge shift that y'all started from moving from marketing being the driver of growth to product and data and experiments and all that stuff. And so I think that's such a good reminder that, fun fact on the social good team, I'm really close friends with the designer that was on my team, his name's Mickey. He was on that team for a while and really enjoyed and yeah, really enjoyed working with you. Fun fact.
turns.zh: 这点说得真好。我差点把这当成理所当然，但你们开启了一场巨大的转变——从由市场驱动增长，转向由产品、数据、实验等等驱动。所以我觉得这是个很好的提醒：说个社会公益团队的小花絮，我和当时在我团队的一位设计师是很好的朋友，他叫 Mickey。他在那个团队待过一阵，非常享受，也很高兴——对，很享受和你共事。小花絮。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Oh, that's so great. I remember Mickey, what is his last name?
turns.zh: 哦，那太棒了。我记得 Mickey，他姓什么来着？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Settler.
turns.zh: Settler。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Okay. Yes, I definitely remember this, yes. And social impact is just one thing that I think I'm really proud of. And again, remember social impact used to be a business thing. You would create this corporate social responsibility part of the company that was very separate from the product and engineering team. (00:32:48): Another thing that we did in the early days was there was a juncture where it was like, "How are we going to translate this site?" And I think we could have taken more of a non-technical traditional approach and had professional translators translate the entire site into the different languages, and instead sort of what the growth team suggested was why don't we build a version of Facebook that allows you to make translations in line? And so the community of people using Facebook at the time who actually knew the product the best could actually insert translations and there was a whole system that we built around how to up-rank the best translations and down-rank, sort of like Wikipedia. And to this day, we have over 100 languages supported. So we're always trying to find these product technology solutions to these sort of traditional problems.
turns.zh: 好。是的，我绝对记得，没错。而社会影响只是我觉得特别自豪的一件事。再次提醒，社会影响以前是件业务的事。你会建立一个和公司产品工程团队完全分离的"企业社会责任"部分。(00:32:48)：早期我们做的另一件事是：到了一个节点，大家想"我们怎么翻译这个网站？"我想我们本可以采取更非技术、更传统的方式，请专业翻译把整个网站翻成不同语言，但增长团队建议的是：我们为什么不做一个允许你"行内翻译"的 Facebook 版本？这样当时最懂这个产品的用户群体，就能直接插入翻译，我们还围绕如何把最佳翻译顶上去、把差的压下去（就像维基百科那样）建立了一整套系统。至今我们支持超过 100 种语言。所以我们一直在尝试用产品、技术的方案，去解决这些传统问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I totally remember that, where it's like you ask your users to help translate the site.
turns.zh: 我完全记得那个，就是你让用户帮忙翻译网站。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back real quick to the activation metric because it's something that a lot of people somewhat misuse and think maybe incorrectly about. So to come up with an activation, as you described, you basically figure out what's the regression of if someone does X, retention increases, and so let's focus on getting them there. And a lot of people struggle with coming up with that metric. Do you have any thoughts on just how important it was to have that very specific activation milestone of seven exact friends in exactly 10 days versus the value of just having anything that is a rallying point for everyone to focus on and drive?
turns.zh: 我想快速回到激活指标，因为很多人对它有点误用，也可能理解得不对。所以，正如你描述的，要得出一个激活指标，你基本是搞清楚"如果用户做了 X，留存就上升"的回归关系，然后我们聚焦把他们带到那里。很多人在想出这个指标上很挣扎。你怎么看：有那个非常具体的激活里程碑——恰好 7 个好友、恰好 10 天——到底有多重要？还是说，只要有某个能让所有人聚焦、去推动的"集结目标"，价值就已经在了？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I think the majority of the value is in the latter, is just having extreme clarity around the goal and that allowed everybody to work towards optimizing the same goal. You're right, we did sort of just pick a point on the curve. I think it could have been any of those. And indeed, as part of preparing for this, I was like, "Was it seven friends in 10 days?" I had to go back and I asked a few people that I worked with back in the day and they were like, "Well, I thought it was 10 in 14." I mean, I think it doesn't matter, it's just that we picked one of them and what mattered there was we had the same goal, what mattered was that it was a retention goal or an activation metric. (00:34:59): And one of the most important things that actually came out of having that goal was building a new user experience. Believe it or not, when we first launched Facebook, I wasn't around then, but in the early days of when it was just a college site, we didn't need a news or onboarding. We didn't need to explain to people that they had to find their friends. They were sort of automagically connected to everyone on the college campus and sort of knew how to use this product, it felt very intuitive. Again, we were college students building a product for other college students. They were sitting next to each other in libraries or at desks and sort of through osmosis understanding how the product worked. (00:35:38): It was more when we launched the ability for teens to register and then work networks, and then in 2006 open registration where we started getting all kinds of people with any email address, before it was .edu or a microsoft.com email address that was required in order to sign up for Facebook and then anyone with any email just could register including people like my dad and my grandma that we realized, wow, in order to get people to this magic moment, how are we going to do that? What's the most effective way that insight resulted in building a new user experience? I remember it was just like step one, upload your profile picture. That was really important so people could find you and know who you were. Step two, find your friends. That's where a lot of the contact importing and people you may know and, "Here are other people at your school and here are mutual friends." That step in the news or experience ultimately became one of the most important drivers of that activation metric that we talked about.
turns.zh: 我觉得大部分价值在后者，就是你对目标有极致的清晰，这让所有人朝着优化同一个目标努力。你说得对，我们其实就是从曲线上随便挑了一个点。我想哪个都行。事实上，为了准备这次采访，我还反问自己"是 10 天内 7 个好友吗？"我得回去问了几个当年一起共事的人，他们说"我以为那是 14 天内 10 个"。我的意思是，我觉得这不重要，关键在于我们挑了其中一个，而在那儿重要的是我们有同一个目标，重要的是它是一个留存目标、一个激活指标。(00:34:59)：而拥有那个目标真正带来最重要的一件事，是催生了一个新用户体验。信不信由你，我们刚推出 Facebook 时我不在场，但在早期它只是个大学网站时，我们不需要动态或引导。我们不需要向人们解释他们得去找好友。他们差不多是自动和校园里所有人连上了，也大概知道怎么用这个产品，感觉非常直觉。再说一次，我们是一群大学生给另一群大学生做产品。他们坐在图书馆或课桌旁彼此相邻，通过耳濡目染就明白产品怎么用。(00:35:38)：更明显的是，当我们开放了青少年注册、然后是职场网络、再到 2006 年开放注册（开始接收任何邮箱地址的人，而以前必须 .edu 或 microsoft.com 邮箱才能注册），任何人只要有邮箱都能注册，包括像我爸我奶奶这样的人，我们才意识到：天哪，为了把人们带到那个神奇时刻，我们该怎么做？最有效的方法是什么？这个洞察促成了构建一个新用户体验。我记得大概就是：第一步，上传你的头像。那非常重要，这样别人能找到你、知道你是谁。第二步，找你的好友。那就是大量"联系人导入""你可能认识的人""这是你学校里的其他人、这是你们的共同好友"的来源。动态或体验里的那一步，最终成了我们聊过的那个激活指标最重要的驱动因素之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you shared that, such a recurring theme on this podcast, the power of onboarding, the value of investing in onboarding and the ripple effects of opportunities there. I love that you also were kind of like the first like, "Onboarding, that's a thing, we need onboarding."
turns.zh: 我超爱你分享这个，这档播客里反复出现的一个主题就是：引导（onboarding）的力量、投资引导的价值，以及那里机会的涟漪效应。我也爱你还算是最早提出"引导，这是个东西，我们需要引导"的人之一。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I know. I mean, I remember the day where I was like, "Do we need to explain to people how to use this? Is it not obvious?" And it's like my dad's like, "I don't understand this whatsoever." My dad would go on to become Facebook's biggest power user because I always beta tested everything with him. But that was not obvious to us at the time in 2006 that we had to explain to people how to use Facebook. (00:37:25): And again, remember that it's fun talking about this because obviously the product has evolved so much, but the principles are relatively the same. It was thefacebook.com, eventually it became facebook.com, but eventually we built a mobile app and then it was mobile first product, and then it was about mobile photos, and then it was about mobile videos. So over time, the technology has really changed, but the core use case that we really need to educate people on, which is how to connect with their friends on Facebook and whatever iteration or product is the same. And so obviously we still have an onboarding today and it's relatively the same principles, like get a profile picture and find your friends.
turns.zh: 我知道。我是说，我记得那天我想"我们需要向人们解释怎么用这个吗？这不明显吗？"然后我爸就说"我这完全看不懂"。我爸后来成了 Facebook 最强力的深度用户，因为我总拿他当一切功能的测试用户。但 2006 年我们并不显然知道，得向人们解释怎么用 Facebook。(00:37:25)：再说一次，聊这个很有趣，因为产品已经演变这么多，但原则相对没变。它从 thefacebook.com，后来变成 facebook.com，然后我们做了移动 App、变成移动优先的产品，然后是移动照片、移动视频。所以随着时间推移，技术真的变了，但我们需要教育人们的核心用例——也就是怎么在 Facebook 上和好友连接，无论产品迭代成什么形态——是不变的。所以显然我们今天依然有引导，原则也大致相同，比如：设个头像、找到你的好友。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those same lines, just maybe a last question around the growth stuff that you worked on for folks that are thinking of driving growth, working on onboarding maybe specifically just are there any lessons from things that worked super well when you were looking to accelerate growth of the Facebook early on that you think people are maybe sleeping on as lepers and tactics that worked back then that might still be really powerful today?
turns.zh: 顺着这条线，关于增长还有最后一个问题，给那些想驱动增长、可能特别想做引导的人：你在早期加速 Facebook 增长时，有没有哪些特别奏效的方法，是你觉得人们可能忽视、但在当年作为战术却依然强大、今天仍可能很有用的？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Well, definitely the understand, identify, execute. I would just ask yourselves, do you have the data that you need to know what you need to do on growth? And if not, definitely take the time to instrument that data. (00:38:49): The thing that, I think we were relatively lucky, I talked about why I was bullish on Facebook in 2005 even was because there was product-market fit. And so for us growth, as much credit as we give to the growth team, I'm actually not sure how much credit we deserve and how much incremental growth we drove above and beyond the fact that this was a product that had product-market fit and we benefited in a huge amount from having high demand for the product. (00:39:23): So at every step, and I talked about the growth team, the projects that we were working on were really at a high level around removing barriers. There were macro barriers, like the first project I worked on was high school students on Facebook, which is an interesting story in and of itself because at that time we almost created a separate website called Facebook High just to keep them separate from the college students. But at that time we were like, "No, this is one graph. This is one community. College students have friends and people they're connected to of all different ages. Why bifurcate the graph?" And obviously we've maintained that principle ever since. (00:40:04): But it was about removing barriers. So you had to be a college student, then you had to be a high school student, then you had to be in a work network, then you had to have any email address. One of the next projects I worked on was not everyone has access to a smartphone, how can we remove the barrier of having access to a smartphone and building more of a rich Facebook experience for someone that was using a feature phone or a lower-end device? Internet.org, what about removing the barrier of having access to the internet or being able to afford a data plan? And so those are the macro barriers that thematically the growth team has worked on. (00:40:40): What I would say is maybe applicable is really the micro barriers. All of the work that we did on growth around optimizing the flows were really about removing micro barriers. One of the things that I thought was just so elegant was after we did that 2009 instrumentation of all the flows, the product flows relevant to growth, what we found is 20% of people aren't actually confirming their email. We tried sending them an SMS, so maybe they would confirm the SMS instead. What we found was a lot of people are actually still clicking on notifications that they're getting, but because it wasn't the specific confirmation email, we weren't able to confirm the account. (00:41:21): And so what we did was allow people to get notifications even as an unconfirmed account, and then if they clicked on any of those notifications, that would count as an account confirmation as well because they proved ownership of the email. It's just removing a micro barrier of having to go find the confirmation email, click it before you can do anything on the site. So I do think we've been relatively lucky in having a lot of high demand That meant that we could focus on just removing micro barriers. And then on the growth team, a lot of the iterations and optimizations were about removing just sort of friction.
turns.zh: 嗯，绝对是"理解、识别、执行"。我就问你们自己：你有没有为了搞清增长该做什么所需的数据？如果没有，一定要花时间去埋点这些数据。(00:38:49)：我觉得我们当时算比较幸运，我之前说过我 2005 年就看好 Facebook，是因为它有产品市场契合。所以对增长来说，尽管我们给增长团队很多credit，我其实不确定我们配得上多少credit，也不确定我们到底在"产品本就有产品市场契合"这个事实之上，额外驱动了多少增量增长——我们大量受益于对产品的高需求。(00:39:23)：所以在每一步，就像我聊增长团队时说的，我们做的项目在高层面上都是关于"消除障碍"。有宏观障碍，比如我做的第一个项目是"Facebook 上的高中生"，这本身是个有趣的故事，因为当时我们差点建一个独立的网站叫 Facebook High，好把他们和大学生分开。但那时我们说"不，这是一张图（graph）、一个社区。大学生有朋友、有各个年龄层的连接对象。为什么要分裂这张图？"而显然我们从此一直坚持这个原则。(00:40:04)：但它关乎消除障碍。先是必须大学生，然后必须高中生，然后必须在职场网络，然后必须任何邮箱都行。我做的下一个项目是：不是每个人都有智能手机，我们怎么消除"拥有智能手机"这个障碍，为用功能机或低端设备的人打造更丰富的 Facebook 体验？Internet.org 呢——消除"能上网或负担得起流量套餐"的障碍？所以这些都是增长团队在主题上处理的宏观障碍。(00:40:40)：我想真正有借鉴意义的是"微观障碍"。我们在增长上做的所有优化流程的工作，本质上都是消除微观障碍。我觉得有一件事特别优雅：2009 年我们把所有相关产品流程埋点之后，发现 20% 的人其实没确认他们的邮箱。我们试着给他们发短信，也许他们就会确认短信。我们发现很多人其实还在点他们收到的通知，但因为那不是特定的确认邮件，我们无法确认账户。(00:41:21)：所以我们做的，是让未确认账户也能收到通知，然后只要他们点了其中任何一条通知，那也算账户确认，因为他们证明了邮箱的所有权。这就消除了"必须去找确认邮件、点了才能用网站"这个微观障碍。所以我确实觉得我们相对幸运，有大量的高需求，这意味着我们能只聚焦于消除微观障碍。然后在增长团队里，大量的迭代和优化其实就是消除各种各样的摩擦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that framework of micro barriers and macro barriers, just thinking about ways to make this accessible to more people and also just helping them get through the flow faster. I also love your point about how a lot of growth teams get a lot of credit for growing a business when really in many ways it could have done really well even without that team potentially because product-market fit was so strong. I think about this with Airbnb honestly as just such after it gets to a certain point, such good product-market fit that who knows what would've happen if there was no one working on growth? It probably would've been okay for a long time.
turns.zh: 我爱这个"微观障碍和宏观障碍"的框架，就是不断想着怎么让更多人能用上，也帮他们更快走完流程。我也爱你的观点：很多增长团队因为业务增长而获得大量赞誉，但其实在很多情况下，就算没有那个团队，业务也可能做得很好，因为产品市场契合太强了。我老实说想到 Airbnb 也是——到了某个节点，产品市场契合这么好，如果没有人做增长，天知道会怎样？可能很长一段时间都还好。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally. And then maybe where we do sort of see the impact is maybe something like the translations thing that we talked about. With the macro barrier, removing the language barrier, and so maybe the approach we took meant that we supported 100 plus languages instead of whatever the professional translators, we have the long tail of languages so that last person who's still speaking a near extinct language can still use Facebook. But yeah, I think that's right. I sometimes think that maybe some of our efforts were really more on the margin of a bigger trend around product-market fit.
turns.zh: 完全同意。然后也许我们真正看到影响的地方，是像我们聊的翻译那件事。有了消除语言障碍这个宏观障碍，所以我们采取的方法意味着我们支持了 100 多种语言，而不是专业翻译能覆盖的那点，我们覆盖了长尾语言——让最后一个还在说濒临消失语言的人也能用 Facebook。但是啊，我想这是对的。我有时会想，我们的某些努力可能真的只是处在一个更大趋势的边缘，那个趋势就是产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final little thing I would just want to highlight again that you said that I think is so important, and I've always thought is true and I love that you confirmed it, is that the activation metric that you all rallied around the biggest value of it wasn't this is exactly the right regression connection to retention, it's more that we have something we are all going to focus on, and that is where most of the impact comes from is let's get more people to that point, whether it's perfectly right or not, it doesn't really matter.
turns.zh: 最后我想再强调一遍你刚说的、我觉得特别重要、也一直认为是真话、而且很高兴你证实了的一点：你们那个用来集结的激活指标，最大的价值并不在于它"恰好是和留存正确的回归关联"，而更在于"我们有了一个所有人会聚焦的目标"，大部分影响正是来自这里——让我们把更多人带到那个点，无论它是否完美正确，其实并不重要。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that. And I think that's really freeing to a lot of people because they're like, "Oh, we don't know if we're going to be as perfect about this versus let's just drive some growth and get people who are good enough thinking on that." Okay, great. (00:43:45): You mentioned Naomi-isms, I want to segue to that. So let me first read a quote. So I asked Adam Mosseri, who is Head of Instagram, what to ask you. I know you guys work together on a bunch of stuff. Here's how he described you, "Naomi is called the conductor here at Meta. She has an incredible ability to handle the most complex projects and problems and bring the right people together to simplify and solve them. She is very firm yet kind. Her standards are extremely high, and she sets the bar." Also many other people that I messaged said very similar things about you, about how you're incredibly good at taking very complex problems and getting shit done, getting them done, simplifying them and getting them done. (00:44:27): So I want to spend some time understanding what you've learned about how to do this well. What are the skills you've collected that allow you to take really complex problems and get to a solution, stay kind but firm and take on these really hard challenges? So maybe just broadly, I'm curious, what are some of these skills that you have built that allow you to do this?
turns.zh: 太爱了。我觉得这对很多人是种解脱，因为他们会想"哦，我们不知道能不能做到那么完美，不如就先驱动点增长、让足够好的人往那方面想"。好，很棒。(00:43:45)：你提到了 Naomi-isms，我想转去聊那个。我先读一句引语。我当初问了 Instagram 负责人 Adam Mosseri，该问你什么。我知道你们在很多事上合作。他是这么描述你的："Naomi 在 Meta 被称为指挥家（conductor）。她有不可思议的能力，能处理最复杂的项目和问题，并把对的人聚到一起，将其简化、解决。她非常坚定却又温和。她的标准极高，并且树立了标杆。"另外我私信问的很多人也都说了非常类似的话，关于你如何极其擅长把非常复杂的问题搞定、简化、做成。(00:44:27)：所以我想花点时间理解，你学到的、关于怎么把这件事做好的东西。你积累的哪些技能，让你能接住真正复杂的问题、得出方案，保持温和却坚定，并接下这些真正艰难的挑战？也许宽泛一点，我好奇，你建立了哪些技能，让你能做到这个？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yeah, well also that's very kind of Adam. I adore Adam obviously, he is one of the tenured people in small group and I've actually gotten the opportunity to work even more closely with him than usual. We recently launched something called Teen Accounts and Adam and I worked very closely on that. (00:45:10): In terms of how I do the things people say that I can do, I really rely on Naomi-isms. Like I said, and actually I refer your podcast out a lot because there isn't just a PM university that I can send people to, there isn't a formal training that people can get to become a product manager, and that's where Naomi-isms came from. It was stuff that I learned on the job from other people, including from Adam, that I found myself repeating over and over again. "A good PM looks for a way to make that more efficient," for me, that was writing them down, people started calling them Naomi-isms. I started sharing them internally. And then I think two years ago, I also started sharing them externally. (00:45:52): Adam referred to me as a conductor, that's one of the Naomi-isms, in my role as Head of Product, I want to educate the PM community about what is PM? It's the most common question I get from PMs and non-PMs, "What do PMs do? What makes a great PM?" And what I say is a PM is a conductor. It's as though the team that you are a PM on is an orchestra. There are many different functions in your team that includes legal policy, comms, data analytics, engineering, design, much like there are many different instruments in an orchestra. And as a PM, your job is to make sure everyone's playing their part correctly, every section in the orchestra is playing their part, but at the same time, they're playing together, they're unified in the music that they're producing and that they're playing at the right tempo. (00:46:48): And a lot of times I think people use music analogies or vocabulary to describe the work, and that includes things like people being in harmony, like a good team, a good PM, a good orchestra is in harmony, they're in sync, they're at the right tempo, they have the right cadence. That's sort of how I imagine what a PM does at work. Important characteristics are the PM is not the star of the show. Indeed, conductors don't even say anything during the performance. And also, I would at the same time give PMs little metronomes and conductor wands. This was something that I used to do when we were smaller., Just to sort of take the analogy way too far.
turns.zh: 对，那个 Adam 说得很客气。我显然很欣赏 Adam，他是 small group 里任职很久的人之一，而且我最近其实有机会比平时更紧密地和他合作。我们最近推出了一个叫"青少年账户"（Teen Accounts）的东西，Adam 和我在这上面合作非常紧密。(00:45:10)：至于我怎么做到人们说的这些事，我真的很依赖 Naomi-isms。就像我说的，而且我确实经常向人推荐你的播客，因为并没有一所"PM 大学"我能把人送去，也没有什么正规培训让人成为产品经理，Naomi-isms 就是这么来的。那是我在工作中、从别人（包括 Adam）身上学到的、发现自己反复在重复的东西。"一个好 PM 会去找让事情更高效的方法"，对我来说，就是把它们写下来，人们开始叫它们 Naomi-isms。我先在内部分享，然后我想是两年前，也开始在外部分享。(00:45:52)：Adam 称我为指挥家，这是 Naomi-isms 之一：作为产品负责人，我想教育 PM 群体"PM 是什么？"这是 PM 和非 PM 问我最多的问题——"PM 做什么？什么造就一个伟大的 PM？"我的回答是：PM 是指挥家。就像你当 PM 的那个团队是一支管弦乐队。你团队里有很多不同的职能，包括法务政策、公关、数据分析、工程、设计，就像管弦乐队里有很多不同的乐器。(00:46:48)：作为 PM，你的工作是确保每个人都正确地演奏自己的部分，乐队里每个声部都在演奏自己的部分，但同时他们在一起演奏、统一于他们正在产出的音乐、并以正确的节奏演奏。很多时候我觉得人们用音乐的比喻或词汇来描述这份工作，包括比如人们"和谐共处"——一支好团队、好 PM、好乐队是和谐的，他们同步、节奏对、韵律对。这就是我想象中 PM 在工作中的样子。重要的特征是：PM 不是舞台上的明星。事实上，指挥家在演出期间一句话都不说。同时，我以前还会给 PM 们发小 metronome（节拍器）和指挥棒。这是我们规模还小的时候我会做的事，就是把比喻用得太过了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. You actually gave him conductor wands and metronomes?
turns.zh: 太好笑了。你居然真的给了他们指挥棒和节拍器？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Oh yeah, just to wave around. Yeah, I love that.
turns.zh: 哦对，就是拿来挥的。是啊，我超爱这个。
