turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: So PM as conductor is sort of how I describe the product management function, but one of the key Naomi-isms that I think is really critical to getting stuff done is what I call extreme clarity. I think our jobs are super hard. Extreme clarity means everyone's on the same page. It definitely doesn't mean that they all agree with each other, but they just have the same understanding of the facts. So we can disagree, but we all believe in the facts, which is that there's A, B, C, our options are X, Y, Z and here are the trade-offs 1, 2, 3. That kind of shared understanding is what extreme clarity is. (00:49:36): That came from a place of just being in many meetings, on many emails, in many situations where I felt like we actually agree on something, the nature of this conflict is a result of misunderstanding. And that seems like an incredible waste of time. And so we want to have extreme clarity so we can just focus our conversations on things when we actually agree, not when we are misunderstanding each other. There are a lot of tactics that I use to drive extreme clarity.
turns.zh: 所以"PM 是指挥家"算是我对产品管理职能的描述，但我认为对"把事做成"真正关键的一个 Naomi-ism，是我所谓的"极致清晰"（extreme clarity）。我觉得我们的工作超级难。极致清晰意味着大家在同一页上。它绝对不意味着大家都同意彼此，而是他们对事实有同样的理解。所以我们可以有分歧，但我们都相信这些事实——也就是有 A、B、C，我们的选项是 X、Y、Z，权衡是 1、2、3。这种共识就是极致清晰。(00:49:36)：它来自这样一种处境：我身在许多会议、许多邮件、许多情境中，觉得我们实际上在某件事上是一致的，而这冲突的本质源于误解。这似乎是在浪费时间。所以我们想要极致清晰，这样我们就能把对话聚焦于我们真正达成一致的地方，而不是互相误解的时候。我用了很多战术来驱动极致清晰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to ask how you do that, that sounds great.
turns.zh: 对，我正想问你是怎么做到的，听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: ... Tactics that I use to drive extreme clarity.
turns.zh: ……我用来驱动极致清晰的战术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to ask how do you do that. That sounds great. How does one get to extreme clarity?
turns.zh: 对，我正想问你怎么做到。听起来很棒。怎么才能达到极致清晰？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: So another name I'm using is canonical everything, so that includes canonical nomenclature, I often talk about canonical nomenclature. One way to ensure extreme clarity is we have the shared vocabulary. I've been in a lot of situations where people are using the same or different words to describe the same or different things, which results in talking past each other. One of the most egregious examples of this is when I was working, I was in a conversation around how our reviewers and global operations were performing, and we were using consistency and accuracy interchangeably. Consistency refers to how often different reviewers agree on the decision. Accuracy refers to how often the decision is correct according to ground truth. Those are very different things. We don't want to optimize for consistency because you could be consistently wrong. We want to optimize for accuracy. (00:50:56): And so that is what canonical nomenclature is literally writing out all the words in their definitions, so when we communicate, we are using the same vocabulary. I really believe in visuals. I think sometimes just having a conversation or a big meeting where people are talking, I'm just not very auditory, I'm a very visual person, it's hard for me to follow along just by listening. I will often have a visual in a meeting. I will leverage that visual to literally real time edit what is being decided. For example, if we have multiple options, I will edit the slide that's being projected to say, "We decided on option one, here are the next steps, 1, 2, 3." A lot of times people are saying, "That's not what I heard. I heard this as a next step, or I heard that as a next step." I love that because that avoids leaving the meeting and being like, "I don't know what we agreed to. I heard this, you heard that." No, actually we haven't agreed upon set of decisions and next steps that we all real time edited and looked at together.
turns.zh: 所以我的另一个说法叫"一切皆权威"（canonical everything），包括"权威命名法"（canonical nomenclature），我常聊这个。确保极致清晰的一个方法是我们有共享的词汇表。我身处过很多情境，人们用相同或不同的词描述相同或不同的事，结果就是各说各话。最离谱的例子之一，是我在讨论我们的审核员和全球运营表现时，大家把"一致性"（consistency）和"准确性"（accuracy）混用。一致性指的是不同审核员对同一个决定的一致程度。准确性指的是这个决定按事实真相看有多正确。这是非常不同的事。我们不想优化一致性，因为你可能"一致地错"。我们想优化准确性。(00:50:56)：所以这就是权威命名法——把所有的词和它的定义都写出来，这样我们沟通时用的是同一套词汇。我非常相信视觉化。我觉得有时光是开个会、一大群人讲话，我有点跟不上，因为我不是听觉型，我是视觉型，光靠听很难跟上。我开会时常会有一份视觉材料。我会用那份视觉材料，实时地去编辑正在被决定的内容。比如，如果我们有几个选项，我会编辑正在投影的幻灯片，写上"我们决定了选项一，接下来的步骤是 1、2、3"。很多时候人们会说"我听到的不是这个。我听到的是这个作为下一步，或者我听到的是那个作为下一步。"我超爱这个，因为它避免了散会后大家"我不知道我们达成了什么。我听到的是这个，你听到的是那个"。不，实际上我们有一组达成一致的决策和下一步，是大家实时一起编辑、一起看的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to double click on that one real quick, so what you're describing for the visual is you're presenting here's our options, here's our three options on a slide. You all decide we're going to go with option two, you edit the slide with a star, here's what we chose, and then maybe change some stuff. And this is exactly to your point of extreme clarity, people can see clearly this is what we're choosing. If they disagree and don't realize that's what's happening, it'll be really clear.
turns.zh: 就着这点再点一下，你说的视觉化就是：你在展示"这是我们的选项，幻灯片上是三个选项"。大家决定走选项二，你用个星号编辑幻灯片"这是我们选的"，然后可能改点东西。这恰恰对应你说的极致清晰——人们能清楚看到"这就是我们在选的"。如果他们不认同、却没意识到正在发生什么，那会非常明显。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: And one thing people make fun of me a lot for that I think is just a great example of extreme clarity is I never use bulleted lists because you can never refer to a bullet. I always use numbered lists because you can always in the visual in a meeting as referenced in number two, I have feedback on that, versus the third bullet, two up from the second, whatever, that is not extreme clarity. So it's very, very small tactical things to bigger things like canonical everything. But I can be a little bit strict.
turns.zh: 还有一件人们常拿我开玩笑、但我觉得正是极致清晰绝佳例子的事：我从来不用项目符号列表（bulleted lists），因为你永远无法引用某一条 bullet。我永远用编号列表（numbered lists），因为你在会议视觉材料里可以说"参考第二条，我对那个有反馈"，而不是"第三条 bullet、从第二条往上数第二条"，那不是极致清晰。所以是非常非常小的战术，到更大的比如"一切皆权威"。但我可能有点严格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that very tactical tip and that is awesome, that's exactly the stuff I look for. Is there any other very nuanced tip along those lines that is helpful in extreme clarity or canonical everything?
turns.zh: 我超爱这个非常实操的小贴士，太赞了，这正是我寻找的那种东西。沿着这条线，还有没有别的、能助益极致清晰或"一切皆权威"的、非常细腻的窍门？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Canonical everything... And stop me if I'm getting too wonky, I can really get into this.
turns.zh: "一切皆权威"……如果我说得太钻牛角尖就打断我，我真的会陷进去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We got a ways to go.
turns.zh: 我们还有很长的路要走。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: When I had a face bursary, along the years people have given me posters and the posters say these Naomi-ism, so extreme clarity is one, canonical everything is another. I think people really associate me with canonical, canonical, canonical. I always want a canonical doc. This came from a place of me I work on a lot of different projects, a lot of times I'm ramping up mid-project, I'm like, "Where can I learn what I need to learn about this project?" I ask five different people, get five different answers, that is unacceptable. Everyone should know exactly where the canonical doc is. That's the one place I can go to get all the information I need about a project and it will link to all the other docs. Of course, I'm sure there's hundreds of docs associated with the project, but there needs to be one canonical doc, and that canonical doc really has to have the basic information that you need to know. (00:54:05): For any project, the basic information that you need to know is what are the discrete areas of work, I call those work streams, this is pretty obvious. Who are the owners on those work streams? So for every work stream there's an owner. Again, it seems pretty obvious. Sometimes I'm like, "Who's owning this?" And it's like people don't know. That's why I think it's very important to have a single-threaded owner. We used to call this a directly responsible individual or a throat to choke. We obviously don't say that anymore. Single-threaded owner, every work stream has a single-threaded owner. Sometimes work streams are really big. You have sub work streams underneath them. Everything canonical needs to recurse, so you should have an owner or an STO for the sub work stream. The other things on the canonical doc are what is the process by which the people on this team work together. (00:54:54): I hate pairwise conversations. I feel like they're a waste of time. I feel like you could have four conversations with four different people or one conversation with all four people. Everyone has the same context. Ideally there's a visual in that meeting and you real time edited it, there is extreme clarity. The canonical doc will have what is the canonical meetings that people have, what is the canonical email list that you're going to use, what is the canonical workplace chat. Let's not reinvent the same audience 10 different times with different permutations of the people on the working team. Let's just have one canonical chat. And then often the canonical doc will have the canonical nomenclature. I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity. A framework is best understood when there's a visual representation of the framework in my mind, and so we'll have canonical visuals and that's what I mean by canonical everything. So anytime I start on a new project, everyone knows to send me the canonical doc.
turns.zh: 我有个 face bursary（面部补助金？此处为口语化表达），这些年人们送过我海报，海报上写着这些 Naomi-ism，所以"极致清晰"是一个，"一切皆权威"是另一个。我觉得人们真的把我跟"权威、权威、权威"联系在一起。我永远想要一份权威文档（canonical doc）。这源于我工作在很多不同项目上，很多时候我是中途接手一个项目，就会想"我该去哪了解这个项目需要学什么？"我问五个不同的人，得到五个不同答案，这不可接受。每个人都该确切知道权威文档在哪。那是获取项目所有所需信息的唯一去处，它会链接到所有其他文档。当然，我知道项目关联着成百上千份文档，但必须有一份权威文档，而且那份权威文档真的得包含你需要知道的基本信息。(00:54:05)：对任何项目，你需要知道的基本信息是：有哪些独立的工作领域，我叫它们"工作流"（work streams），这挺显然的。这些工作流上谁是负责人？所以每个工作流都有个负责人。这看起来也挺显然。有时我会问"谁在负责这个？"然后发现大家不知道。这就是为什么我觉得有个"单一线程负责人"（single-threaded owner）非常重要。我们以前叫它 DRI（directly responsible individual，直接责任人），或者"可以掐的脖子"（throat to choke）。我们现在显然不这么说了。单一线程负责人，每个工作流都有一个。有时工作流很大，下面还有子工作流。(00:54:54)：一切权威的都得递归，所以你应该给子工作流也配个负责人或 STO（single-threaded owner）。权威文档上的其他内容是：这个团队的人一起协作的流程是什么。我讨厌一对一的对话（pairwise conversations）。我觉得那是浪费时间。我觉得你可以和四个人分别聊四次，或者和四个人一起聊一次。大家有同样的上下文。理想情况下那次会议里有一份视觉材料，你实时编辑它，就有极致清晰。权威文档会写：有哪些权威会议、用哪个权威邮件列表、用哪个权威职场聊天群。别用工作团队人员的不同排列组合，把同一批受众重复发明十次。我们就用一个权威聊天群。然后权威文档通常还会有权威命名法。我真心相信框架，它能驱动极致清晰。一个框架最好理解的方式，是它在我脑中有个视觉化的呈现，所以我们会有权威视觉材料，这就是我说的"一切皆权威"。所以每当我开始一个新项目，每个人都知道把权威文档发给我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. If you come into a that you've given that's really gnarly and complex, what do you find are the first couple things you do that make a big dent on helping everyone align and understand what happens, what they should be doing and what they should be prioritizing?
turns.zh: 我超爱这个。如果你接手一个你给过建议、特别棘手复杂的项目，你发现最先做的哪几件事，能大幅帮助大家对齐、搞清楚该做什么、该优先什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: A lot of times I'm simplifying. A lot of times there isn't a canonical doc and so I'll go through the process of creating that, but I think that really falls under the simplification thing. I often go into a project, everyone's operating at a PhD level, I'm coming in at a kindergarten level, and so I need to understand... It's almost like all of this complexity we're at a PhD level, I need to create the curriculum, go back to basic building blocks for the kindergarten level, how do I explain that and understand this project at a kindergarten level. It doesn't mean I want to oversimplify, that's not what a simplifier does. They're not oversimplifying, but what they are doing is identifying the most basic building blocks of a complex problem and then unfolding, or revealing or building on top of them additional complexity and details as you go along. (00:57:06): And so sometimes I talk about a school pyramid, but I need to establish the kindergarten curriculum and then the elementary school curriculum and then the high school curriculum and then the college curriculum, and then we can operate at the PhD level. But oftentimes people on the project are at really different levels of understanding or complexity. And until we have what we call the school pyramid, the curriculums for every level of the project, it's really hard to make progress. A lot of times that process of simplification will often identify what are the most important things to deal with on the project.
turns.zh: 很多时候我在做简化。很多时候并没有权威文档，所以我会走一遍创建它的过程，但我觉得那其实属于简化那一类。我经常进入一个项目时，大家都在"博士 level"运作，而我是以"幼儿园 level"进来，所以我需要理解……这就像所有这些复杂性我们在博士 level，我需要创建课程，回到基本的积木块、幼儿园 level，我怎么解释、理解这个项目？这不意味着我想过度简化，那不是"简化者"做的。他们不是过度简化，但他们做的是：识别一个复杂问题最基础的积木块，然后随着推进，在其上展开、揭示或构建额外的复杂性和细节。(00:57:06)：所以有时我聊"学校金字塔"（school pyramid），但我得先建立幼儿园课程、再小学课程、再中学课程、再大学课程，然后我们才能在博士 level 运作。但项目上的人常常处在很不同的理解水平或复杂度上。直到我们有了所谓的学校金字塔——每个层级对应的课程——才真正能取得进展。而那个简化的过程，往往能识别出项目上最重要、该处理的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what I'm hearing is when you come into a project and the way you simplify is you start putting together a doc that describes these things you're talking about, here's the work streams, here's the owners, here's the process, here's our canonical meeting style, and that reveals here's what matters most and where there's confusion.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是：你进到一个项目，你简化的方式就是开始整理一份文档，描述你说的这些东西——这是工作流、这是负责人、这是流程、这是我们的权威会议风格——而这会揭示出什么最重要、哪里有困惑。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes, yes. Yeah, that is. And a lot of times what needs to happen in the project is sometimes there's a strategy or an execution issue and sometimes there's a people or a process issue. I would say 80% of the time I think it's a people or process issue. And that refers to not having the right people on the project, or having the right people but not having the right process by which they work together, a strategy or execution issue. When we get to that, I first try to tackle those or in general I think it's really important to have perfect execution. I want to make sure a project is perfectly executing, because only then can we really reevaluate whether or not this strategy is right or wrong. We're in the worst of all worlds where we are imperfectly executing and therefore, at the end of the day, the project might fail, but we don't know why. (00:59:02): Is it because the strategy was right or wrong or is it because the execution was poor? The ideal case is the strategy was right and you perfectly executed on it. The next best case scenario is the strategy was wrong, but you perfectly executed on it, because then you learned the strategy was wrong. Revamp the strategy and try again.
turns.zh: 对，对。是的。很多时候项目里需要发生的，有时是战略或执行问题，有时是人 or 流程问题。我想 80% 的情况下是人或流程问题。那指的是：没有把对的人放在项目上，或者人有但对了、却没有让他们协作的正确流程，才导致战略或执行问题。当遇到这个，我会先尝试解决那些；总体而言，我觉得"完美执行"真的很重要。我想确保一个项目在执行上是完美的，因为只有那样我们才能重新评估这个战略到底对不对。最糟的情况是：我们执行得不完美，于是到头来项目可能失败，但我们不知道为什么。(00:59:02)：是因为战略对错，还是因为执行糟糕？理想情况是战略对、且你完美执行了它。次优的情况是战略错、但你完美执行了它，因为那样你学到了战略是错的。重整战略再来一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're really in the PM part of my brain. I feel like most PMs listening are like it has clean documents, really simple processes, there's one person to charge, it links to everything. It just feels good.
turns.zh: 你真的戳中了我作为 PM 的那根神经。我觉得大多数听这档播客的 PM 会想：有干净的文档、真正简单的流程、有一个人负责、链接到一切。就是感觉很好。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally. And, again, sometimes I feel the need to defend that the process is not for process' sake, it's ultimately to help us all move faster and work better. So hopefully that comes through. But I deeply believe that it is through this approach that we can move faster. And you have to prove that nobody wants more process and more meetings and more, but my goal is that with this we're actually simplifying process and getting less meetings and just making things clearer and ultimately moving faster.
turns.zh: 完全同意。而且，再说一次，有时我觉得需要为"流程不是为了流程本身"辩护一下，它最终是为了帮我们所有人都更快前进、更好地工作。所以希望这点能体现出来。但我深信，正是通过这种方法我们才能更快。你得证明——没人想要更多流程、更多会议、更多东西，但我的目标是，用这个我们实际上在简化流程、减少会议、让事情更清晰、最终更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to read another quote from another one of your co-workers, Charles Porch, he's vice president of global partnerships at Instagram and he basically said what we've been talking about, some of the biggest strategic bets and biggest swings Meta has made have had Naomi at the helm. No one can hurt cats, drive clarity, and get to outcomes more seamlessly than she can. She's legendary within Meta for her canonical documents.
turns.zh: 我读另一段你同事 Charles Porch 的引语，他是 Instagram 全球合作副总裁，他基本说了我们一直在聊的：Meta 做过的一些最大战略押注和最大动作，都是 Naomi 在掌舵。没人能比她更会"赶猫"（herd cats）、驱动清晰、更顺畅地拿到结果。她在 Meta 内部因她的权威文档而传奇。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just following this thread a little bit further, what's the gnarliest project that you've worked on that would be a good example of you coming in and helping simplify and get it over the finish line?
turns.zh: 也许顺着这条线再往下一点，你做过最棘手、能作为"你进去帮忙简化、把它带到终点"好例子的项目是什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Well, Charles may be thinking of the most recent project that we worked on. I don't know if it's necessarily the gnarliest, but it's definitely one of the most cross-functional projects that I've worked on before. Basically every team at the company in some way works on youth. And last week we actually launched teen accounts, which was a very complex project. Again, it involved the Instagram team, the central youth team, the different teams working on various aspects of this, every function, legal policy, comms, marketing product. And I think we definitely leveraged a lot of these Naomi-isms. And just to give you a sense of what teen accounts is, it was basically putting all teens into the safest settings by default on Instagram. And the reason I'm working on this, I work across multiple teams at Facebook, so obviously Adam is the head of Instagram and I work closely with him on this, like I was referring to yesterday. (01:02:02): But this is something, these teen accounts, is something that we are thinking about how we expand to the other apps that we have, including Facebook and WhatsApp and Threads. And I tend to work on projects that are across our family of apps and future platforms, and that's why I was involved in this. But basically what teen accounts does is put teens in these safest settings. It's super focused on trying to address parents' biggest concerns around their teens on social media. This has obviously been a really big topic. We've had a lot of these features and tools. What this launch did is simplify things, standardize things, and add a lot more functionality that gives parents control. (01:02:42): I think the thing you really need to know is that for under 16-year-olds, if they want to change any of these defaults, they're going to have to get their parents' permission. And so it's interesting that we're really going to create an incentive for teens to get their parents involved and to actually set up parental supervision, especially because one of the default settings is a private account. So there's tens of millions of teens that currently have public accounts today that we are going to automatically transition to private accounts unless they get their parents' permission to stay public. And so it's a relatively big shift, fundamental change for how Instagram works for teens, and I would say one of the more complicated projects that I've worked.
turns.zh: 嗯，Charles 可能想的是我们做过的最近那个项目。我不确信它一定最棘手，但它绝对是我做过最跨职能的项目之一。基本上公司里每个团队都以某种方式在做青少年相关的事。上周我们刚刚推出了青少年账户（teen accounts），这是个非常复杂的项目。它涉及 Instagram 团队、中央青少年团队、做各方面工作的不同团队，每个职能——法务政策、公关、市场、产品。我觉得我们绝对大量借用了这些 Naomi-isms。给你一个概念，青少年账户是什么：它基本是把所有青少年默认放进 Instagram 上最安全的设置里。我为什么参与这个？我在 Facebook 多个团队间工作，显然 Adam 是 Instagram 负责人、我和他在上面紧密合作，就像我昨天提到的。(01:02:02)：但这件事——这些青少年账户——是我们正在思考怎么扩展到我们其他 App 的，包括 Facebook、WhatsApp 和 Threads。而我倾向于做跨我们应用家族和未来平台的项目，这就是我参与的原因。但基本上，青少年账户做的是把青少年放进这些最安全的设置。它超级聚焦于解决父母对青少年社交媒体最大的担忧。这显然是个大话题。我们已有大量这类功能和工具。这次发布做的是：简化事情、标准化事情，并加入大量让父母能掌控的功能。(01:02:42)：我觉得你真正需要知道的是：对于 16 岁以下的人，如果想改任何这些默认设置，他们得获得父母许可。所以这很有意思，我们真的在创造一种激励，让青少年把父母卷进来、真正建立家长监督，尤其是因为其中一个默认设置是"私有账户"。所以现在有数千万今天还是公开账户的青少年，我们会自动把他们转到私有账户，除非他们拿到父母许可保持公开。所以这对 Instagram 怎么为青少年运作是个相当大的转变、根本性的改变，我想这也是我做过最复杂的项目之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and it just launched, right?
turns.zh: 对，而且它刚发布，对吧？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a new father, I'm excited for you all to be working on these sorts of things. I don't need it yet, but I'm glad it's going to be there. And it's funny how Meta and Facebook is in this world where people complain about teens using social media and then you work on making the product better for teens and kids using social media, and then it's like, "Facebook's getting teens on social media." There's no way to make it feel good to people. No matter what you do, people are going to complain. That's what-
turns.zh: 作为一个新手爸爸，我很高兴你们在做这类事。我现在还用不上，但我很高兴它会在那儿。而且很有趣，Meta 和 Facebook 处在一个人们抱怨青少年用社交媒体、然后你们又努力把产品做得对青少年和小孩更好的世界里，然后人们又说"Facebook 在让青少年用社交媒体"。无论你做什么，都没办法让人感觉好。人们总会抱怨。这就是——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally. And I think the goal of this launch was to orient ourselves and really there's a lot of complaints, there's a lot of different voices. I think we just are focused on parents. We think parents know best. Every kid is different and parents know their own kid the best. So that has been our north star in terms of the approach here. When I talk about teen accounts, as product people I think one thing that you would appreciate is the thing that I think is really important when it comes to teens on the internet is really having an understanding of how old someone is when they're using our apps. And it's important that we know how old they are because then we can put them in an age-appropriate experience. So now we have teen accounts, we want to put all teens into teen accounts. (01:04:49): We all know sometimes teens lie. That's been the biggest feedback that we've been getting is teens are really smart, they're going to find workarounds, they're going to be creative, they're going to lie about their age. And as a product person, the way that I think this should really work is that instead of everyone entering... Teens use, on average, 40 apps, instead of Instagram and the other 39 apps that teens use trying to verify the age of the person using their app is for two companies to do this, which is Apple and Google, they do collect the age, they should make that available to developers. And we ask for information from the device all the time with user consent, can Instagram have access to your camera, can Instagram have access to your location information? Apps should be able to ask, can Instagram have access to your birthday? And that would, I think, elegantly from a product perspective, from a simplification perspective, from a privacy preserving perspective and what's easiest for parents, that would be the right product solution to solve this problem around age that we're all trying to grapple with right now. (01:05:56): And there's a lot of stuff that we're doing. Part of the reason that this project was so complicated, and I mentioned the age team, is we're building classifiers to try to predict how old people are based on not just the age that they've stated, but based on who they're talking to, what kind of content they're looking at, what the age of the people they're connected to is, do we think that this is actually an adult like they say, or is it really a teen. And so we're doing a lot to try to predict age or prevent people from lying about their age, but I think this would be a really big win for the industry.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我觉得这次发布的目标是让我们自己定个方向，确实有很多抱怨、很多不同的声音。我想我们就是聚焦于父母。我们认为父母最懂。每个孩子都不同，父母最懂自己的孩子。所以那一直是我们的北极星。聊到青少年账户，作为产品人，我想你会欣赏的一点是：关于互联网上的青少年，我认为真正重要的一件事，是搞清楚用我们 App 的人到底几岁。知道他们几岁很重要，因为那样我们才能把他们放进适合其年龄的体验。所以现在我们有青少年账户，我们想把所有青少年都放进青少年账户。(01:04:49)：我们都知道有时青少年会撒谎。这是我们收到的最大的反馈——青少年很聪明，他们会找变通办法、会发挥创意、会对年龄撒谎。而作为一个产品人，我觉得这事真正该运作的方式是：与其让每个人都输入……青少年平均用 40 个 App，与其让 Instagram 和其他 39 个青少年用的 App 都去验证用它们 App 的人的年龄，不如让两家公司来做这事，就是 Apple 和 Google，它们确实收集年龄，它们应该把年龄开放给开发者。(01:05:56)：我们一直在向设备要信息（用户同意前提下）——Instagram 能访问你的相机吗、能访问你的位置信息吗？App 应该能问：Instagram 能访问你的生日吗？而我觉得，从产品角度、从简化角度、从保护隐私角度、以及对父母最省力角度，那都会是解决这个问题（我们都在努力应对的年龄问题）的正确产品方案。我们还在做很多事。这个项目之所以这么复杂、我提到年龄团队的原因之一，是我们正在构建分类器，试图预测人们的年龄——不只基于他们陈述的年龄，还基于他们在和谁聊天、看什么内容、他们连接的人年龄多大，来判断这到底像他们说的那样是个成年人，还是其实是个青少年。所以我们做了大量工作去预测年龄或防止人们谎报年龄，但我觉得这对整个行业会是个巨大的胜利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense to me.
turns.zh: 我觉得说得通。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Okay. Thank you, Lenny.
turns.zh: 好。谢谢你，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to close out this portion in this chapter of our conversation on Naomi-isms, I know something else that you're really good at that I've heard from a few people is running meetings, something that a lot of people always want to get better at. Any tips? What have you learned about running a great meeting?
turns.zh: 那么在结束我们对话中"Naomi-isms"这一章之前，我知道你还特别擅长一件事、我也从几个人那儿听说，就是主持会议——很多人都一直想做得更好。有什么窍门？你从主持一场好会议中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: A meeting is a high value and it's high cost amount of time, and then I want to make sure it's as productive as possible. What I will do is send an agenda 24 hours prior to the meeting. That agenda will include a pre-read. I've talked to people who if the pre-read is not attached to the calendar invite or associated with a meeting at least 24 hours in advance, they will cancel the meeting. That just goes to show we want everybody in the meeting to have full context, have read the pre-read. Often what will happen in the previous 24 hours is because we're all sending pre-reads on Google Slides, there will be a lot of conversation and questions that get hashed out leading up to the meeting. During the meeting, like I said, I think it's really important for a group of people to be looking at something and anchoring people on something. (01:07:48): If somebody joins the meeting, say, five minutes late, they should know exactly where in the agenda you are in the meeting and what is being discussed based on catching up from the visual that's being projected. Usually a meeting can be and hopefully a meeting is really either is a decision meeting. So if there is a decision, I need three options and I need a recommendation that should hopefully help focus the meeting. And then, like I said, I will real-time edit the visual such that we document and have extreme clarity on what is the option that we agreed on and any next steps that we also agreed to. (01:08:28): After the meeting, anyone who wasn't in the meeting, that's fine because within 24 hours post-meeting I will send the notes, reply all to the meeting invite and send the notes. So just tactically, I use the calendar invite as the canonical unit by which to handle all of this communication because a lot of times meetings are one-offs, there isn't an existing email or chat thread that maps perfectly to the audience of the meeting, so for me that is the meeting or the calendar invite. So I'll click on the calendar invite, reply all, include the pre-read, pre-meeting, and then do this reply all again post-meeting 24 hours with the notes and the decisions and the next steps.
turns.zh: 会议是一段高价值、也是高成本的时间，所以我想确保它尽可能有产出。我会做的是：在会议前 24 小时发议程。议程里会包含一份会前阅读（pre-read）。我聊过有些人，如果会前阅读没附在日历邀请里、或没提前至少 24 小时关联到会议，他们会直接取消会议。这正说明：我们希望每个进会议的人都有完整上下文、都读过会前阅读。往往在前 24 小时里，因为大家都在 Google Slides 上发会前阅读，会有一大堆对话和问题在会前就被厘清了。会议期间，就像我说的，我觉得让一群人看着同一个东西、以此把大家锚定在某件事上，真的很重要。(01:07:48)：如果有人迟到五分钟进来，他们应该能根据正在投影的视觉材料，准确知道会议进行到议程的哪一块、在讨论什么。通常一场会议能、也希望真的能是"决策会议"。所以如果有个决策要做，我需要三个选项、需要一个推荐，这应该能帮会议聚焦。然后，就像我说的，我会实时编辑视觉材料，这样我们就记录并达成了极致清晰：我们同意的是哪个选项、以及我们也同意的下一步是什么。(01:08:28)：会议之后，任何没在会上的人也没关系，因为会后 24 小时内我会发笔记，对会议邀请"回复全部"并附上笔记。所以战术上，我用日历邀请作为处理所有这些沟通的"权威单元"，因为很多时候会议是一次性的，并没有一个现成的邮件或聊天串完美对应会议的受众，所以对我来说那就是会议、或日历邀请。所以我会点开日历邀请、回复全部、附上会前阅读（会前），然后再在会后 24 小时用笔记、决策和下一步再做一次回复全部。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. So many very specific tactics here. I love it. This is food for my brain. I love the always have three options and a recommendation, that's such a simple thing to recommend, but such a powerful way of operating as a PM, just like, "Here are the options, here's what I recommend, here's why."
turns.zh: 我超爱这个。这么多非常具体的战术。我爱死了。这是给我大脑的食物。我超爱"永远给出三个选项加一个推荐"，这是个如此简单的建议，却是作为 PM 运作的超强方式，就像"这是选项、这是我推荐的、这是为什么"。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Oh, one thing I forgot that I learned from Guy Rosen, he is our chief security officer, is when you have three options and a recommendation, in terms of evaluating the options, I don't love pros and cons. It's a flat list of text. It's hard to just get the big picture from that. Oftentimes we'll use a traffic light. That means that the three options are three rows. The columns in the table will be criteria by which to evaluate the options. Those could either be functions. So for example, if I have three options as the rows, column one could be the legal perspective, column two could be the policy perspective, column three could be the privacy or product perspective. Alternatively, the columns could map to different criteria like what we're optimizing for. So it could be the user experience, it could be the engineering feasibility, it could be the internal complexity, whatever are the criteria should be laid out in the columns. (01:10:31): And then obviously it should be color-coded, red, yellow, green based on how it stacks up against those criteria. And what this allows is to get back to the point of the visual is you can quickly look at the three options, see where's the most red, and rule that out. Ideally, the recommendation has some combination of the more green or yellow than the other options. And then obviously within these cells you can spell out the specific rationale for the coloring. But I think this is a really good way to run a meeting and just create extreme clarity around how you're evaluating the options in a way that a flat list of pros and cons just doesn't.
turns.zh: 哦，我忘了一件从 Guy Rosen 那儿学的——他是我们的首席安全官——就是当你有三个选项加一个推荐时，在评估选项方面，我不爱用"优点缺点"（pros and cons）。那是一份平铺的文字清单，很难一眼看清全貌。我们常用"红绿灯"（traffic light）。意思是三个选项是三行。表格里的列是用来评估这些选项的标准。这些列可以是各种职能。比如，如果三行是三个选项，第一列可以是法务视角，第二列是政策视角，第三列是隐私或产品视角。或者，列也可以对应不同的标准，比如我们优化的目标。可以是用户体验、工程可行性、内部复杂度， whatever 是标准就铺在列里。(01:10:31)：然后显然它应该按这些标准上的表现来配色——红、黄、绿。这让你能回到视觉化的点：你可以快速扫三个选项，看哪里最红，把它排除掉。理想情况下，推荐项在某些组合上比其他选项更绿或黄。然后显然在这些格子里你可以写出具体配色的理由。但我觉得这是运行会议、就"你怎么评估选项"达成极致清晰的绝佳方式，而平铺的优缺点清单做不到这点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What other podcasts would have this level of detail of how to run a discussion on a decision? And this is exactly what people want to hear, so I love it. So product market fit for listeners of this podcast. I love it. I love it. And obviously the reason this is more effective is it's not just like, "Here's a quick sentence on the pro and con." It's like, "Here's what I actually think this is good or bad for the things that matter to the business."
turns.zh: 还有哪个播客会有这种程度的细节，讲怎么主持一个决策讨论？而这正是人们想听的，所以我超爱。对这档播客的听众来说，这就是产品市场契合。我爱。我爱。而显然它更高效的原因是，它不只是"这里一句关于优缺点的短话"，而是"这是我真正认为它对业务重要的事是好是坏"。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: That's exactly right.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that makes tons of sense.
turns.zh: 所以这非常说得通。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: It also gives people a framework to plug into. A lot of times the creation of a pre-read for these discussions involves many different people from many different teams and functions. If you have a traffic light, they can own filling out their cell, they can own the rationale behind the legal position on option one, two, and three. And, in general, I'm super into frameworks that allow people to plug into and clearly represent their point of view.
turns.zh: 它也给了人们一个可以plug into 的框架。很多时候，为这些讨论写会前阅读，涉及很多来自不同团队和职能的人。如果你有个红绿灯表，他们可以负责填自己那格，可以负责写选项一、二、三上法务立场的理由。总体而言，我超爱那些能让人们plug into、清晰表达自己观点的框架。

turns.zh: 我超爱。最后一个问题，完全不同的话题。我看到《华尔街日报》一篇关于你如何锻炼、以及你的锻炼习惯对你生活和职业有多重要的报道。现在，大多数人的锻炼习惯上不会有《华尔街日报》的报道，尤其一个科技工作者。我知道这对你的工作很重要，他们写说这基本帮你把工作做得更好。对那些想投入锻炼、多锻炼、以及到底怎么做到的人，有什么建议？因为你的建议是：这真的让你在工作和生活上更出色。

turns.en: People are always like, "What are you training for?" And I'm like, "I'm training for life." I have four musties, it is eat, sleep a long time, and exercise. Those are the things that I need in order to perform. And the other areas of my life seems pretty obvious, but until recently I actually did not prioritize sleep. My boyfriend is actually super into sleep and we have the Eight Sleep, we have eye masks, we have blackout shades, we have good sleep hygiene, and so I'm getting much better at that. But exercise is something that I've always been on top of. Alone time is also a musty for me because I'm an introvert, I need that time to recharge, otherwise I think I get weird around people. (01:13:28): In terms of how I prioritize it, it's a non-negotiable or table stakes, every morning I have to work out. I am also lucky enough to work in an environment where I can wear workout clothes to work, which I often do. I think working out is sure the hour of the day that I'm doing my exercise, but I also view, like I said, life is a workout, performing at work is a workout. I need to be able to move. I need to feel comfortable. It's very physical, I think, especially if you're trying really hard to be a conductor, and I'm running around with a metaphorical conductor wand, I need to be able to move. A while ago, and that's what the Wall Street Journal article was about, I set a goal of doing five pull-ups. I'd read somewhere in an article that less than 1% of women can actually do. I think having a goal is really helpful. (01:14:22): That's something that I worked on, and anyone can do this truly if you train for it. I think it's potentially more technique for me than strength per se, and I worked up towards that goal. I think exercise, in addition to all of the physical benefits, primarily has a mental health benefit I think for me. And also there are just a lot of lessons that I think I take from exercise. For example, I think being able to do five pull-ups taught me I can do hard things in this really narrow, measurable way, which gave me confidence in other aspects of my life.
turns.zh: 人们总问"你在训练什么？"我就说"我在训练生活"。我有四个"必须品"（musties），就是吃、睡很久、独处、锻炼。这些是我发挥所需的东西。我生活的其他方面似乎挺显然，但直到最近我才真正把睡眠当回事。我男朋友其实超级迷睡眠，我们有 Eight Sleep、有眼罩、有遮光帘、有很好的睡眠卫生，所以我在这方面好多了。但锻炼是我一直都在坚持的。独处对我也是必须，因为我是内向者，我需要那段时间充电，否则我觉得自己在人面前会变怪。(01:13:28)：至于我怎么把它排优先级，它是"不可商量"或"底线"，每天早晨我必须锻炼。我也很幸运能在可以穿运动服上班的环境工作，我也常那么穿。我觉得锻炼当然是我在做运动的那一小时，但我也像说的那样，把生活当成锻炼、把工作表现当成锻炼。我需要能动起来。我需要觉得舒服。这非常身体化，我想，尤其当你拼命想当个指挥家、拿着隐喻的指挥棒跑来跑去，我需要能动。不久前，也就是《华尔街日报》那篇文章写的，我定了个做 5 个引体向上的目标。我在某篇文章里读到，能做到的女性不到 1%。我觉得有个目标真的很有帮助。(01:14:22)：那是我努力过的，而且任何人只要训练都能真正做到。我想对我而言可能更多是技巧而非纯粹力量，我朝着那个目标练上去了。我觉得锻炼，除了所有身体益处，对我主要的还是心理健康益处。而且我从锻炼里学到很多东西。比如，我觉得能做 5 个引体向上，以一种很窄、可衡量的方式教会我"我能做难的事"，这给了我生活其他方面的信心。

turns.zh: 完全同意。有很多研究说，哪怕环境光也会降低睡眠质量。所以我想这就是遮光帘和眼罩能帮忙确保真正黑暗的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was just watching a podcast and the advice there is even your smoke alarm with a little light is too much light. You need to cover that up to create real darkness and why not just wear an eye mask? You don't have to worry about any of that.
turns.zh: 对，我刚在看一个播客，那边的建议是连你烟雾警报器上那点小光都太亮了。你得把它盖住来创造真正的黑暗，那为什么不干脆戴个眼罩？你就不必操心任何这些了。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, and then one thing I didn't mention when you're talking about the conductor, the PM as a conductor, that's exactly the metaphor I've always used my entire career when people ask me about what is product manager? So we're alike.
turns.zh: 好，然后有件事我刚没提，就是你聊指挥家、PM 是指挥家时，那正是我整个职业生涯一直用的比喻，当人们问我"产品经理是什么"。所以我们很像。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I have all these slides of here's the PM and it's like a symphony and the conductor standing there.
turns.zh: 对，我有所有这些幻灯片，讲 PM 就像交响乐、指挥家站在那儿。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Lenny, do you know how happy that makes me? Because I feel like sometimes people are like, "That sounds crazy," but the fact that you actually came to that same conclusion makes me... Why did you come to that conclusion? I'm just curious
turns.zh: Lenny，你知道这让我多开心吗？因为我觉得有时人们会"这听起来疯了"，但事实是你也得出了一样的结论，让我……你为什么得出这个结论？我就是好奇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because as you said, the PM's not making the thing. They're just helping each of the people who are the most talented at their very specific skill do the best possible work and their back is to the audience. They're trying to stay out of the way even though they come in, everyone claps for them, the outstanding event, and then in theory they could step in a little bit to help out when they can pinch it on design here and there and research here and there, probably not engineering. So those are the reasons and they're not in charge. The chair wind violinist is the actual person that's making the music and the best at this thing.
turns.zh: 因为就像你说的，PM 不是在做那个东西。他们只是帮每个在自己特定技能上最有天赋的人，做出尽可能好的工作，而且他们的背对着观众。他们试图不挡路，尽管他们进场时大家都为他们鼓掌、是最出彩的时刻，然后理论上他们可以在这里那里稍微搭把手——在设计上、在研究上这儿那儿 pinch 一下，大概不是工程。所以这些就是原因，而且他们不是管事的。首席小提琴手才是真正在奏乐、最擅长这事的人。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: It's so great to hear somebody else talk about this too. Thank you. And I think that that is really how I view my role and what I do and I think maybe just hearing you talk about it reminded me why I think I put so much emphasis on just elevating the people on my team and the people around me and candidly, one of the development areas for me, and it could be downstream because I do have this analogy of how to be a PM, is that the growth feedback or the constructive feedback for me is really learning when to lead from the front more. Maybe when to be less of a quiet conductor that's really elevating the first chair violinist and be more front facing. (01:18:39): I think a lot of my approach and my leadership style is really leading through the people on my team and helping grow them. And a lot of times I think that they're dedicated, they're experts, they know particular areas. Obviously as a head of product, I manage a portfolio of different projects of which each of them has the incredible leader on it. And so oftentimes I'm just really trying to lead from behind and help them be as successful as possible. But there is a time and a place when maybe that silent conductor needs to take more of a vocal and front facing role.
turns.zh: 听到别人也聊这个太好了。谢谢。我想这确实是我看待自己角色和所做的事的方式，而且我想，听你聊这个让我想起，为什么我把这么多强调放在"提拔我团队和周围的人"上。坦白说，我的一个发展领域——可能是因为我有这个"怎么当 PM"的比喻——就是成长反馈或建设性反馈对我而言，真的是学会"什么时候从前面领导"。也许什么时候少当那个安静的、只提拔首席小提琴手的指挥家，多当面向前。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know exactly what you mean. I had the same problem when I was a PM because there's always this fear that PMs in charge and telling everyone to do. And so I had the opposite of like, "Okay, and that's not me. I'm going to just let you do the things you think are best and I'll just make sure the best ideas come to the surface," and I have to learn exactly the same thing. Sometimes people just want you to point them in the right direction and make the decision in the end. And the best PMs are people that have the best opinions about what is going to work, how intuition of what users need, have strong product sense and all that stuff. I've had this post that I'm trying to work on along these lines where there's this reaction to PMs aren't the CEO of the product. (01:19:56): They're just like... No, don't call yourselves that. I think it's the opposite. I think PMs actually should think of themselves as the CEO of the product, not in terms of they are in charge and can fire people and manage people, but they're the closest heuristic for what the CEO and the founder wants. They think of what does the business need, what is going to help the customers, what's going to help us grow? And I think the PM is the closest to that role and so I think it's important to think of that role as that even though you're not technically in charge.
turns.zh: 我完全知道你的意思。我当 PM 时也有同样的问题，因为总有一种恐惧，觉得 PM 是管事的、指挥所有人。所以我的反应是相反的——"好，那不是我。我会让你做你认为最好的事，我只是确保最好的想法浮上来"，而我也得学完全一样的事。有时人们就是想让你给他们指个方向、最后做决定。最好的 PM 是那些对"什么会奏效"有最好见解的人，对用户需要什么有直觉，有强的产品感等等。我有个一直在琢磨的帖子，沿着这条线——有一种反应是"PM 不是产品的 CEO"。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: And maybe you could call it something different, but I totally agree with that sentiment. I think we were trying to push against the criticism that PMs were bossing everybody around, but actually I think you-
turns.zh: 也许你可以叫它别的，但我完全同意那个情绪。我想我们当时是想反击"PM 在指挥所有人"的批评，但其实我觉得你——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's baggage there.
turns.zh: 这里有沉重的包袱。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: There's baggage there. I call it, there's something called the great non-technical. There was a period of time at Facebook where I think the PMs really had to prove their value to the engineers and show that we were not slowing things down with all this extra process. You can imagine an engineer hearing me talk about how to run a meeting and all the canonical docs and just be like, "What? This sounds terrible." So yeah, we had to prove that, but I actually do think the PM is the closest to really channeling what the CEO or the founder wants. Another thing that I've worked on and that I'm working on is really developing a much stronger first-party perspective. It's not enough for the PM to run this people in process that we talked about. Obviously I love that stuff. I lean that way, but at the end of the day, a PM cannot outsource their perspective or delegate their thinking through people and process. (01:21:46): And so for me that has been a learning curve and I am trying to, as someone who's very consensus driven, I want to hear all the different opinions from all the different people. I can still do that. I can still through people in process talk to all the different folks working on a project, hear their first party perspectives and then use all of that to synthesize my own because it will be unique given my role on the team and just what I'm trying to optimize for and really make sure that I both develop that first-party opinion and communicate it clearly. And like you said, the best PMs I think can do it all.
turns.zh: 这里有沉重的包袱。我称之为"伟大的非技术者"（the great non-technical）。Facebook 有过一段时期，我想 PM 们真的得向工程师证明自己的价值、证明我们不是用所有这些额外流程在拖慢事情。你能想象一个工程师听我聊怎么主持会议、所有权威文档，然后"什么？这听起来糟透了"。所以我们得证明，但我确实觉得 PM 最接近于真正传递 CEO 或创始人想要的东西。另一件我做过、正在做的事，是真正培养更强的"第一手视角"（first-party perspective）。对 PM 来说，光跑我们聊的"人和流程"是不够的。显然我爱那些。我倾向那一边，但归根结底，一个 PM 不能把他们的视角外包、不能透过人和流程来 delegating 他们的思考。(01:21:46)：所以对我来说那是个学习曲线，我正努力——作为一个非常共识驱动的人，我想听到所有不同的人不同的意见。我仍然可以那么做。我仍然可以通过人和流程，和项目上所有不同的人聊、听他们的第一手视角，然后用所有这些综合出我自己的，因为鉴于我在团队里的角色、以及我想要优化的东西，它会是独特的，并且真正确保我既发展出那个第一手观点、又清晰地沟通它。就像你说的，我想最好的 PM 能把这些全做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to follow this thread, one thread further, because this is something I think a lot of product managers work on and are told to work on, is there anything you've found to be helpful in building this skill in yourself that might be helpful to folks that are working on it?
turns.zh: 顺着这条线再往下一点，因为这是很多产品经理在修炼、也被要求修炼的东西，你有没有发现对自己培养这个技能有帮助、也可能对正在修炼的人有帮助的事？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I'm lucky enough because I have a big team. I have someone who helps me schedule my time and I used to goal that person and goal our work together on just being as efficient as possible. But now what I am goaling that person and what we're trying to accomplish here is giving me as much time to develop a first-party point of view. And so what is the most effective way to do that? And for me it is having two to three hour blocks of time where I can actually sit, think, have space, but maybe something that's different about me than other people is its very, very helpful for me to talk to maybe one or two people, not be in a big meeting with 40 people, trusted people. (01:23:28): I have an incredible person on my team that I talk to that I think really helps me clarify my thinking. And so to go back to the beginning, just I'm trying to find blocks in my day that I can spend time thinking and also within those blocks, they don't have to be alone time. They can also be scheduling my chief of staff and my head of data to bounce ideas off of as a sounding board because that is the process that I know best for me in terms of really developing a first party perspective.
turns.zh: 我很幸运，因为我有个大团队。有个人帮我安排时间，我过去给那个人定的目标、以及我们一起工作的目标，是尽可能高效。但现在我给那个人定的目标、我们想达成的，是给我尽可能多的时间去发展第一手视角。那最有效的做法是什么？对我来说，是有两到三小时的整块时间，我能真的坐下来、思考、有空间，但也许我和别人不同的点是：对我和一两个人聊特别有帮助，而不是开个 40 人的大会，是信任的人。(01:23:28)：我团队里有个超棒的人，我会和他聊，我觉得真的帮我厘清思路。所以回到开头，我正试图在我一天里找整块时间，能花时间思考，而在那些整块时间里，不必是独处。也可以安排我的参谋长（chief of staff）和我的数据负责人，把他们当回声板（sounding board）来碰撞想法，因为那是我最了解的、发展第一手视角的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good tip. It makes sense if you're just spending all your day coordinating in meetings, checking things, reviewing things, you have no time to actually think about what you think is the right move and answer and strategy and next step. And so that's a really good tip. If you're finding that you don't have time to think about what you think is the right solution and the right strategy and the right product decision, fine, just block time to think about this stuff. I have these deep work slots in my calendar. I've written about this a few times where it's three hours and the invite, I don't know if you can do this these days, but it was just, if you book time during the slot, I will slap you. Nobody did.
turns.zh: 太好的窍门。说得通——如果你整天就在会议里协调、检查、审阅，你根本没时间真正思考你认为正确的举措、答案、战略和下一步是什么。所以这是个很好的窍门。如果你发现自己没时间思考你认为正确的解决方案、正确的战略、正确的产品决策，好，就block时间去思考这些事。我日历里有"深度工作"时段。我写过几次这个，就是三小时，邀请上写——我不知道现在还能不能这么干——就是"如果你在这个时段约时间，我就扇你"。没人干过。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: That's amazing. And I think for me, some people might need three hours on their own. I think for me, and I don't know about you, talking things through with one or two people really helps me as well. So sometimes it was almost quite challenging for me to think of going into a room by myself for three hours and then I was just going to figure it out on my own. This is like, and I don't know how people help people think strategically the best, but it doesn't have to necessarily be alone.
turns.zh: 太了不起了。我想对有些人，可能需要自己独处三小时。但我想对我和你（不确定你），和一两个人把事聊透也特别帮我。所以有时对我来说，想到自己进房间独处三小时然后自己搞定，简直颇有挑战。我不知道人们怎么最能帮人战略性思考，但它不一定非得是独处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great tip. Just have a sparring partner.
turns.zh: 太好的窍门。就是找个"陪练"（sparring partner）。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone who is just interested in exploring ideas and not just have a clear agenda. I love that. Okay, Naomi, I love this tangent we went on as we were wrapping up.
turns.zh: 一个只是有兴趣探索想法、而不是有个清晰议程的人。我超爱。好，Naomi，我爱我们收尾时拐的这个小弯。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I know, totally.
turns.zh: 我知道，完全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was amazing. There was a lot of good stuff that we covered there, but I know you have to run. So before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that we haven't covered that you wanted to cover or share?
turns.zh: 那太了不起了。我们覆盖了很多好东西，但我知道你得走了。所以在进入我们超兴奋的快问快答（lightning round）之前，还有什么我们没覆盖、你想覆盖或分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Honestly, I think I just did it. I didn't even realize I wanted to talk about that, but it just all came out.
turns.zh: 老实说，我想我刚刚都说了。我甚至没意识到我想聊那个，但它就全冒出来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. I love that. Those are the best nuggets. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我超爱。我爱这个。那些是最好的金句。说到这儿，我们到了超兴奋的快问快答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，你最常推荐给其他人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: I really love narrative nonfiction, so I like the Eric Larson books. They're a very compelling and page turning way to learn about history. I recently read Devil in the White City and there was also one about Churchill's first year by Eric Larson. Another book that just the canonical book that I often recommend is Sapiens. I think he's a great example of what we talk about when we talk about simplifiers. He took a very complex subject, which is all of human history and tried to pull out the nuggets. I think his thesis that what differentiates humans from other forms of life is really our ability to tell and believe in myths or stories, and he cites money and religion as examples, but also there's a graphic novel version of Sapiens and so he almost has the PhD level and then he literally has the high school level, which is a graphic novel version. (01:26:57): He also has Unstoppable Us, which I think is a kid's version, and so clearly here is someone who is a master. There's a James Clear thing that a friend, Shirley, told me about where it's like if you're a beginner, you have ignorant simplicity and intermediate has functional complexity, and then a master of a topic has profound simplicity. And that's what I feel like Noah Yuval Harari really has because he can go all the way up and down this cool pyramid in terms of explaining this really complex topic.
turns.zh: 我超爱叙事性非虚构（narrative nonfiction），所以我喜欢 Erik Larson 的书。它们是用非常吸引人、让人手不释卷的方式学历史。我最近读了《白城魔鬼》（Devil in the White City），还有一本 Erik Larson 写的关于丘吉尔第一年（Churchill's first year）的。另一本我常推荐的权威书是《人类简史》（Sapiens）。我想他是我们在聊"简化者"时很好的例子。他拿了一个极复杂的主题——整个人类历史——试图提炼出金块。我觉得他的论点是：人类区别于其他生命形式的地方，正是我们讲述并相信神话或故事的能力，他举了金钱和宗教为例，而且《人类简史》还有个graphic novel（漫画）版，所以他几乎既有博士 level、又有高中 level（漫画版）。(01:26:57)：他还有《Unstoppable Us》，我想是儿童版，所以显然这里有个大师。有个 James Clear 说的东西，是我朋友 Shirley 告诉我的：如果你是个初学者，你有无知的简单（ignorant simplicity）；中级有功能性的复杂（functional complexity）；而一个主题的大师有深刻的简单（profound simplicity）。我觉得这就是 Noah Yuval Harari 真正拥有的，因为他能在这座很酷的金字塔上上下下，解释这个极复杂的主题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I heard about him is that he goes on a one-month meditation retreat every year where it's just him silent meditation retreat, and people ask him, "How do you have time to do that when you have so much work to do?" He's like, "The only way I'm able to achieve these books where I synthesize all of human history into a story is because I do that. Because I can clear my mind and just be."
turns.zh: 我听到的关于他的事是，他每年去一个月的冥想闭关，就他自己、安静的冥想闭关，人们问他"你有这么多工作，怎么有时间做这个？"他说"我之所以能写出这些把整个人类历史综合成故事的书的唯一原因，就是因为我做这个。因为我能让心智清空、只是存在"。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: And Lenny, to our previous conversation, that is how he himself is best. That's what he needs to do. I might need two to three hours a day and a sparring partner, Noah Yuval Harari needs a month in silent meditation.
turns.zh: 而 Lenny，回到我们之前的对话，那正是他自己最好的方式。那是他需要做的。我可能需要每天两到三小时和一个陪练，Noah Yuval Harari 需要一个月的安静冥想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great point. Everyone has their own way of unlocking their brain. On Devil in the White City, a fun fact. When I read that, I was like, "I need to go to Chicago and see the stuff that they wrote about in this book about the World's Fair." And so I went to Chicago and-
turns.zh: 好观点。每个人有自己解锁大脑的方式。说回《白城魔鬼》，有个小花絮。我读它时想"我得去芝加哥看看书里写的世博会那些东西"。于是我去了芝加哥，然后——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: You did?
turns.zh: 真的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because of that book, yes.
turns.zh: 因为那本书，对。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Wow. Have you read the Splendid in the Vile?
turns.zh: 哇。你读过《Splendid in the Vile》吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. That was the-
turns.zh: 读过。那是——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Churchill.
turns.zh: 丘吉尔。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: About the Telegram, right? Yeah. Right?
turns.zh: 关于那个电报（Telegram），对吧？对？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Oh, no, it was was Churchill's first year, but he has like six books. I haven't read all of them.
turns.zh: 哦不，那是丘吉尔的第一年，但他有大概六本书。我没全读过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I think it was either that one or it was something about a telegram. I did read... It was less good though, is was what I find. I found the Devil in White City was-
turns.zh: 好。我想要么是那本，要么是某个关于电报的。我读过……没那么好，这是我发现的。我觉得《白城魔鬼》是——

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: The best.
turns.zh: 最好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was the best. Amazing. Okay, we'll keep going. Second question, do you have a favorite movie or TV show you've recently watched that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最好的。太了不起了。好，我们继续。第二个问题，你最近有没有特别喜欢、刚看过的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: We just watched Shogun. I thought it was really good. Have you seen it?
turns.zh: 我们刚看了《幕府将军》（Shogun）。我觉得超好。你看过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have, yes. I loved it. Very gruesome but amazing.
turns.zh: 看过，对。我超爱。非常血腥但超棒。

turns.speaker: Naomi Gleit
turns.en: Yeah. I was. I had to cover my eyes for some of it. And then we also, the movie that we just watched was Dune Two.
